definitions.definition: A child deserted by his biological or adoptive parents or guardians, who has been declared as abandoned by the Committee after due inquiry.
definitions.plain_english: An abandoned child is one whose parents or guardians have left them behind with no intention of returning to care for them. The child is officially recognised as 'abandoned' only after a Child Welfare Committee investigates the situation and formally declares it so. This status unlocks special legal protections and pathways, including the possibility of adoption.
real_world_examples: A newborn infant left outside a government hospital in Mumbai with no identification or note, and after the Child Welfare Committee conducts an inquiry and cannot trace any parent or guardian, the child is formally declared abandoned.

A five-year-old child found wandering alone at a railway station in Chennai for several days; the Railway Protection Force hands the child to the Child Welfare Committee, which after due inquiry — including police verification and public notices — declares the child abandoned when no family comes forward.

A toddler left at the doorstep of a temple in Lucknow by unknown persons; the temple priest reports the matter to the Child Welfare Committee, which investigates and, upon finding no traceable family, formally declares the child abandoned to enable placement in a Specialised Adoption Agency.

A seven-year-old girl found living on the streets of Kolkata after her biological father remarried and the stepmother drove her away; the Child Welfare Committee, after inquiry confirming the father refuses to take custody, formally declares her abandoned under the Act.

A child with a physical disability left at an orphanage gate in Hyderabad by an adult who provided false contact details and could not be traced; the Committee's due inquiry confirms desertion and the child is declared abandoned, making her legally free for adoption proceedings.
what_it_covers: A newborn or older child left in a public or private place by biological parents with no intention of return, subsequently declared abandoned by the Committee after inquiry.
A child deserted by adoptive parents who refuse to maintain or claim the child, where the Committee has conducted due inquiry and issued a formal declaration.
A child left by a guardian (not a biological or adoptive parent) who has completely forsaken custody and responsibility, confirmed as abandoned through the Committee's inquiry process.
A child found without any traceable parent or guardian after reasonable inquiry by authorities, formally declared abandoned to enable legal permanency planning including adoption.
what_it_excludes: A child who is voluntarily surrendered by parents through the formal surrender deed process — such children are classified as 'surrendered child', not abandoned.

A child temporarily separated from parents due to disaster, migration, or hospitalization, where the parents retain intention and capacity to return — absence alone without intent to desert does not constitute abandonment.

A child whose parents or guardians are missing but actively being searched for, and no formal declaration has yet been made by the Committee — the label 'abandoned' only attaches after due inquiry and formal declaration.
A child placed voluntarily in an observation home or children's home by a parent seeking temporary care — voluntary placement with continued parental intent does not amount to abandonment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a child is formally declared 'abandoned' by the Child Welfare Committee determines their eligibility to be declared 'child legally free for adoption' under Section 38, enabling adoption proceedings under Sections 56, 58, 65, and 66; without this declaration, the child cannot be lawfully placed for adoption. It also triggers the State's duty to provide institutional care, rehabilitation, and protection under the Act, and governs registration and placement obligations of Specialised Adoption Agencies under Section 66 and related provisions.

definitions.definition: "Abandoned child" means a child deserted by his biological or adoptive parents or guardians, who has been declared as abandoned by the Committee after due inquiry.
definitions.plain_english: An abandoned child is one whose biological parents, adoptive parents, or legal guardians have left them behind without care or support. The label is not automatic — a Child Welfare Committee must formally investigate and officially declare the child as abandoned. This status unlocks specific legal protections and pathways such as adoption and institutional care for the child.
real_world_examples: A newborn infant found wrapped in cloth and left outside a government hospital in Patna with no identifying information about the parents — after the Child Welfare Committee conducts an inquiry and no parents come forward, the child is formally declared abandoned.

A five-year-old girl found wandering alone at a railway station in Mumbai with no adult accompanying her; despite police efforts to trace her family over several weeks, no guardian is located and the Committee declares her an abandoned child.

An adoptive couple in Delhi who took a child informally stops responding to calls, leaves the child with a neighbour indefinitely, and cannot be traced; the Committee, after due inquiry, declares the child abandoned by the adoptive parents.

A three-year-old boy left at the doorstep of a child care institution in Chennai by an unknown person with a note but no contact details; after the Committee's inquiry fails to identify or locate the biological or legal guardians, the child is declared abandoned.

A child found in a flood-affected village in Assam with no surviving or traceable relatives, whose parents are confirmed dead and no guardian claims responsibility; the Committee, after inquiry, declares the child abandoned, making the child eligible for adoption through a Specialised Adoption Agency.
semantic_tags: child legally free for adoption pathway
what_it_covers: A newborn or young child left in a public place or at an institution by biological parents who cannot be traced after due inquiry by the Committee.
A child deserted by adoptive parents who have legally adopted the child but subsequently abandoned all responsibility for the child's care and upbringing.
A child deserted by a legal guardian (other than biological or adoptive parent) where the Committee, after inquiry, confirms the desertion and declares the child abandoned.
A child left behind during a natural disaster or civil unrest where parents or guardians are confirmed absent and no one claims guardianship, leading to a formal Committee declaration.

A child voluntarily surrendered on roadside or public premises by guardians who later cannot be located, following which the Committee completes due inquiry and issues a formal declaration of abandonment.
what_it_excludes: A child whose parents are temporarily missing but are subsequently traced and resume care — the Committee declaration has not been made and parental ties remain intact.

A surrendered child who has been voluntarily given up by parents through a formal surrender deed to a Child Welfare Committee or Specialised Adoption Agency, as such a child falls under the distinct category of 'surrendered child' rather than an abandoned child.

A child whose parents are alive, identifiable, and willing to resume care even if the child was temporarily left without supervision — desertion and official declaration of abandonment are both absent.
An orphan child whose both parents are confirmed dead — such a child falls under the category of 'orphan' rather than abandoned child, as there is no act of desertion involved.

A child placed temporarily with a relative or foster family by parents who intend to reclaim the child — temporary placement without intent to permanently desert does not constitute abandonment under this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Once a child is formally declared an 'abandoned child' by the Child Welfare Committee under Sections 38 and 2, the child becomes eligible to be declared 'child legally free for adoption' under Section 38, unlocking the adoption process through a Specialised Adoption Agency under Sections 59 and 62, and entitles the child to all protections, care, and rehabilitation services under the Act including placement in a Children's Home. Without this formal declaration, the child cannot be processed for adoption, and institutions cannot lawfully treat the child as legally free for adoptive placement.

definitions.definition: Abduction, for the purposes of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, refers to the acts described under sections 359 to 369 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, as applied mutatis mutandis to any child or minor under the age of eighteen years, including compelling or inducing a person under eighteen years by force, deceit, or other means to go from any place.
definitions.plain_english: Abduction means forcibly or fraudulently taking away or luring a child (anyone below 18 years) from one place to another. It covers situations where a child is moved through threats, deception, or physical force without lawful authority. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, all Indian Penal Code rules about abduction apply specially to protect children.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi lures a 14-year-old girl with promises of a job in another city and takes her away from her home without her parents' knowledge or consent, constituting abduction under this Act.
In Mumbai, a group of traffickers forcibly bundle a 16-year-old boy into a vehicle and transport him to another state to be used in forced labour, which amounts to abduction of a child.
A woman in Chennai uses deception to convince a 10-year-old child that her parents have sent her to take the child away, and removes the child from school premises — this qualifies as abduction.

In rural Uttar Pradesh, a child marriage facilitator forces a 15-year-old girl to accompany him to a different district for an illegal marriage by threatening her family, constituting abduction under Sections 84 read with IPC sections.

A stepparent in Kolkata, without any legal right or court order, takes a 12-year-old child from the lawful custody of the biological mother to another state against the child's will, amounting to abduction.
what_it_covers: Forcibly compelling a child under 18 years to move from one place to another against their will or without lawful consent.
Inducing a minor through deceit, enticement, or fraudulent means to leave a place of safety or lawful custody.
Taking or luring a child from the custody of a lawful guardian using threats, misrepresentation, or coercion.
Transportation of a child across districts or state borders through force or deception for any unlawful purpose including trafficking or forced marriage.
Acts of abduction committed against a child by a stranger, acquaintance, or even a family member without legal authority.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary movement of a child of sufficient maturity who is not compelled, deceived, or threatened in any manner.
Lawful transfer or movement of a child by a parent, guardian, or competent authority acting under a valid court order or legal authority.
Acts committed against adults aged eighteen years and above, which are governed solely by the IPC without the specific protections of the Juvenile Justice Act.
Consensual movement of an emancipated or legally married individual above the age of eighteen, even if previously classified as a minor.
Custody disputes resolved under family court orders where a parent acts in accordance with a legitimate court-sanctioned arrangement.
definitions.why_it_matters: The application of abduction provisions under Section 84 means that any act of abduction against a child under eighteen triggers enhanced legal obligations including mandatory reporting, police intervention through Child Welfare Police Officers, and referral to the Child Welfare Committee, while also forming the basis for prosecution under the IPC as extended to children. Establishing that abduction occurred determines whether the victim qualifies for special protective measures, rehabilitation, and restoration under the Juvenile Justice framework.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 'abetment' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in Section 107 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860). Whoever abets any offence under this Act, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, shall be punished with the punishment provided for that offence.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or conspiring with someone to commit a crime under this law. A person is guilty of abetment if they instigate another to commit an offence, engage in a conspiracy to commit it, or intentionally assist in its commission. If the crime actually happens as a result of that help or encouragement, the abettor faces the same punishment as the person who directly committed the offence.
real_world_examples: A father in Mumbai instructs his elder son to take the younger sibling to traffic signals to beg for money daily; the father is guilty of abetment under Section 76 read with Section 87, even though he did not personally place the child at the signal.

A guardian in Delhi, knowing that a trafficker plans to employ a child in forced begging, provides the child's address and facilitates the trafficker's access to the child — the guardian is liable for abetment of the offence of employing a child for begging.

A NGO worker in Chennai conspires with a shelter home manager to conceal a child who has been subjected to abuse within the institution, thereby abetting the suppression of the offence and obstructing the child's restoration — both face equal punishment.

In Kolkata, a landlord knowingly allows his premises to be used for recruiting children for begging rackets and actively encourages the operator — his deliberate facilitation constitutes abetment under Section 87 of the Juvenile Justice Act.

A relative in Hyderabad who has actual charge of a child coerces the child into begging by threatening withdrawal of food and shelter; even if the relative does not physically deploy the child, the intentional instigation amounts to abetment under Section 76(2).

A social media influencer in Bengaluru creates content glorifying child begging and directs followers to a network that employs children for organised begging — such wilful instigation and publicity support can constitute abetment of the offence.
semantic_tags: conspiracy to commit JJ Act offence
what_it_covers: Instigation by a parent, guardian, or any person who actively encourages or directs another to commit an offence under the Juvenile Justice Act.
Engaging in a prior conspiracy with one or more persons to commit a defined offence under the Act, such as employing children for begging.
Intentional aiding — through physical assistance, provision of resources, information, or access — that facilitates the commission of an offence under the Act.
A person who has actual charge or control over a child and abets the commission of offences such as employment of the child for begging under Section 76(2).
Any act of deliberate concealment or wilful omission that directly enables another person to commit an offence under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Mere presence at the scene of an offence without any prior conspiracy, instigation, or intentional assistance does not constitute abetment.
Accidental or unknowing assistance — where the person had no knowledge that their act would facilitate the commission of an offence under the Act — is excluded from abetment liability.

The child victim who is made to beg or is subjected to an offence is explicitly excluded from being treated as a child in conflict with law under the proviso to Section 76(2), and cannot be held liable for abetment.
General moral disapproval or failure to report an offence, without any active instigation or intentional facilitation, does not meet the threshold of abetment as defined under IPC Section 107.
Offences committed entirely independently without any causal link to the alleged abettor's act are excluded — the abetted act must be committed in consequence of the abetment.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether a parent, guardian, relative, or third party who did not directly commit an offence under the Juvenile Justice Act can nonetheless be prosecuted and punished with the same severity as the primary offender. It also triggers the consequence under Section 76(2) that a guardian found guilty of abetment is declared unfit under Section 2(14)(v), leading to the child's removal from their custody and placement before the Child Welfare Committee for rehabilitation.

definitions.definition: "Actual charge" is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; however, as used in Section 76, it refers to the cost or expense actually and directly incurred in the maintenance, care, treatment, or rehabilitation of a child placed in any child care institution or placed under the supervision of a fit person or fit facility, as distinguished from any notional, estimated, or administrative overhead cost.
definitions.plain_english: "Actual charge" means the real, out-of-pocket money that is spent to look after a child who has been placed in a care home or under the supervision of an authorised person. It is the true cost of food, shelter, clothing, medical care, and other necessities provided to the child. This amount can be recovered from the person who is legally responsible for the child, such as a parent or guardian, if they are capable of paying.
real_world_examples: A child in conflict with law is sent to an observation home in Mumbai for three months pending inquiry. The Board orders the parents to pay the actual charge of Rs. 4,500 per month incurred by the home for the child's food, clothing, and medical expenses.

A child in need of care and protection is placed in a Children's Home in Chennai run by a registered NGO. The District Magistrate calculates the actual charge at Rs. 6,000 per month and directs the financially capable biological father to reimburse the State Government.

A surrendered child is temporarily placed with a fit person in Lucknow. The Committee assesses the actual charge incurred by the fit person for groceries, school supplies, and doctor visits, and orders the biological parents—who later resurface and have means—to pay back the amount.

A child victim of trafficking is kept at a place of safety in Kolkata during court proceedings. The actual charge for her stay, including counselling sessions and vocational training, is computed by the institution and submitted to the court for possible recovery from the offender under Section 76.

A juvenile declared to be in conflict with law is placed in a special home in Hyderabad for reformation. The Juvenile Justice Board directs the guardian, who is employed and solvent, to contribute toward the actual charge for the child's upkeep during the period of stay.
what_it_covers: Direct expenses incurred by a child care institution such as food, clothing, bedding, and toiletries provided to the child during their stay.
Medical and healthcare costs, including hospitalisation, medicines, and psychological counselling, actually spent on the child placed in a fit facility or place of safety.
Educational materials, vocational training supplies, and rehabilitation programme costs directly charged to maintain the child within an observation home or special home.
Expenses paid to a fit person for the day-to-day maintenance and care of a child placed under their supervision by the Board or Committee.
Transportation and administrative costs directly attributable to the individual child's care and not general overhead of the institution.
what_it_excludes: Notional or estimated costs that were not actually incurred but projected as administrative overhead of running the institution as a whole.
Salaries and emoluments of staff members of the child care institution that are not directly and specifically attributable to the care of a particular child.
Capital expenditure or infrastructure costs of the institution, such as building maintenance, depreciation, or purchase of equipment, which are not charged to any individual child.
Costs incurred after the child has been discharged, restored to family, or transferred to another institution, which cannot be attributed to the period of actual placement.
Fines or penalties imposed as punishment, which are distinct from the charge for actual maintenance and care of the child.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of 'actual charge' under Section 76 triggers the financial liability of a parent, guardian, or any person responsible for the child, compelling them to reimburse the State or institution for costs of the child's care; if not paid, it may be recovered as an arrear of land revenue. It directly governs whether the State or a voluntary organisation bears the financial burden of child maintenance or whether that burden is shifted to the responsible adult.

definitions.definition: 'Adoption' means the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from his biological parents and becomes the lawful child of his adoptive parents with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities that are attached to a biological child.
definitions.plain_english: Adoption is a legal process where a child is permanently removed from the care of his or her biological parents and becomes the full legal child of new parents, called adoptive parents. The adopted child gets all the same rights as a biological child would — including inheritance rights — and the adoptive parents take on all parental responsibilities. This is a permanent and irreversible legal change in the child's family status.
real_world_examples: A couple in Mumbai who cannot have biological children approach a Specialised Adoption Agency and, following CARA guidelines, legally adopt a two-year-old girl from a children's home in Pune; she permanently becomes their lawful daughter with full inheritance rights.

An orphaned boy in Delhi, declared legally free for adoption by the Child Welfare Committee after his parents died in an accident, is adopted by a non-resident Indian couple settled in Canada under inter-country adoption provisions, severing all legal ties with his biological family.

A surrendered infant girl in Chennai, whose biological mother signed a surrender deed citing inability to care for her, is placed through in-country adoption with a Tamil Nadu family, who then obtain an adoption order from the court making her their legal child.

A child with disability living in a Specialised Adoption Agency in Kolkata is adopted by a prospective adoptive couple who specifically registered to adopt a child with special needs; post-adoption, the child is entitled to the adoptive parents' property and carries their family name legally.

An overseas citizen of India residing in Singapore adopts a child from a recognised adoption agency in Hyderabad through the CARA-authorised process, after which the child's biological parents have no further legal claim or responsibility over the child.
what_it_covers: In-country adoption where Indian prospective adoptive parents adopt an orphaned, abandoned, or surrendered child declared legally free for adoption by the Child Welfare Committee.

Inter-country adoption where non-resident Indians, overseas citizens of India, persons of Indian origin, or foreign nationals adopt a child from India through CARA and an authorised foreign adoption agency.

Inter-State adoption where prospective adoptive parents from one Indian state adopt a child from a child care institution in a different state, facilitated through CARA's centralised adoption resource information and guidance system.
Adoption of a child with special needs or disability by prospective adoptive parents who have specifically registered for such children under the adoption regulations.

The full bundle of legal consequences that follow upon completion of adoption, including the child's right to inherit from adoptive parents and the extinguishment of all legal ties with biological parents.
what_it_excludes: Foster care arrangements, where a child is placed temporarily with a foster family but legal parenthood does not transfer and the child retains legal ties with biological parents.

Guardianship orders under other laws (such as the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890) where an adult is appointed to care for and manage the affairs of a child without permanently severing ties with biological parents or conferring full child status.
Sponsorship of a child, which provides financial or other support for a child's education and welfare without any change in legal parentage or family status.

Informal or customary arrangements where a child is taken in and raised by relatives or community members without undergoing the formal legal process prescribed under the Act and adoption regulations.

Restoration of a child to biological parents or guardians, which is the opposite of adoption and involves reuniting the child with existing legal family rather than creating a new permanent legal family relationship.

definitions.definition: "Adoption agency" means a Specialised Adoption Agency recognised under section 65, or any other agency recognised by the Authority for the purpose of facilitating the adoption of children, and includes a recognised adoption agency as referred to in the adoption regulations framed under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An adoption agency is an officially recognised organisation that is authorised to facilitate the legal adoption of children in India. It acts as an intermediary between children who are legally free for adoption and prospective adoptive parents, ensuring that the entire process follows the rules set by the government. These agencies are registered and monitored by the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) to protect the best interests of children.
real_world_examples: A Specialised Adoption Agency registered under CARA in Mumbai facilitates the adoption of an orphaned child by a couple from Pune, managing documentation, home study reports, and court filings throughout the process.

An NGO in Chennai that is recognised by CARA as an adoption agency maintains a roster of children legally free for adoption and matches them with prospective adoptive parents after conducting background checks and counselling sessions.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Kolkata facilitates an inter-country adoption, coordinating with CARA and the receiving country's Central Authority to place a surrendered child with overseas citizens of India residing in Canada.

A government-recognised adoption agency in Jaipur receives a child declared abandoned by the Child Welfare Committee, registers the child on the Child Adoption Resource Information and Guidance System (CARINGS) portal, and initiates the matching process with prospective parents.

An adoption agency in Hyderabad is penalised under Section 80 of the Juvenile Justice Act for conducting illegal adoption placements without following the prescribed adoption regulations, highlighting the statutory obligations such agencies must comply with.
what_it_covers: Specialised Adoption Agencies recognised under section 65 of the Juvenile Justice Act and registered with CARA to facilitate domestic adoptions.
Agencies authorised by CARA to facilitate inter-country adoptions, including coordination with authorised foreign adoption agencies and overseas prospective adoptive parents.
Recognised NGOs or voluntary organisations that are empowered to receive surrendered or abandoned children, maintain their care, and process them for adoption under CARA regulations.
Any agency formally listed and approved under the adoption regulations framed by the Authority for the purpose of matching children legally free for adoption with prospective adoptive parents.
what_it_excludes: Unauthorised or unregistered private individuals or entities that arrange child placements without formal recognition from CARA, even if they claim to provide adoption services.
Children's Homes, observation homes, or other child care institutions that may house children but are not specifically recognised or registered for the purpose of facilitating adoptions.

Authorised foreign adoption agencies based outside India, which are separate entities governed by the provisions applicable to inter-country adoption and operate under their own country's Central Authority.
Hospitals, medical institutions, or maternity homes that may be involved in surrendering or receiving newborns but are not themselves recognised as adoption agencies under the Act.
Individual lawyers, social workers, or middlemen who may assist in paperwork but do not hold institutional recognition as an adoption agency under CARA or the adoption regulations.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a recognised adoption agency determines whether it can lawfully place children for adoption; operating as an unrecognised adoption agency or conducting adoption outside this framework attracts criminal liability under Section 80 of the Act, which prescribes imprisonment and fines for illegal adoption practices. Only a recognised adoption agency can legally receive, register, and process children legally free for adoption, and non-compliance with adoption regulations by such agencies can result in de-recognition and prosecution.

definitions.definition: An adoption order is an order passed by the District Magistrate under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, issued upon an application filed by a Specialised Adoption Agency, upon being satisfied that the adoption is for the welfare of the child, due consideration has been given to the wishes of the child, and no payment has been made in consideration of the adoption, thereby legally formalising the transfer of the child to the prospective adoptive parents.
definitions.plain_english: An adoption order is an official legal document issued by a District Magistrate that formally makes a child the legal son or daughter of the adoptive parents. Once this order is granted, the child gets all the rights of a biological child in the adoptive family. It is the final step that legally completes an adoption process under the Juvenile Justice Act.
real_world_examples: A couple from Pune applies through a Specialised Adoption Agency to adopt a three-year-old orphan girl from a children's home in Maharashtra. After the home study report is approved, the agency files an application before the District Magistrate, who, after verifying the welfare of the child, issues an adoption order legally making the child their daughter.

A Non-Resident Indian couple settled in the United States wishes to adopt an abandoned child from India. After the Authority matches them with a child through a Specialised Adoption Agency, the agency files an application before the District Magistrate, and the resulting adoption order is sent to the Authority to obtain a passport and visa for the child to travel abroad.

A single woman in Delhi, aged 38, applies through a Specialised Adoption Agency to adopt a five-year-old surrendered child. After pre-adoption foster care placement and scrutiny by the District Magistrate to ensure no monetary consideration was involved, an adoption order is passed, granting her full parental rights over the child.

A couple in Chennai seeks to adopt two biological siblings to keep them together. The Specialised Adoption Agency files an application before the District Magistrate. The Magistrate, after hearing the matter and being satisfied about the children's welfare, issues an adoption order for both siblings simultaneously, legally placing them with the adoptive family.

An overseas citizen of India residing in Singapore adopts a physically disabled child declared legally free for adoption. The District Magistrate issues the adoption order after the Specialised Adoption Agency files the requisite application, enabling the child to travel to Singapore and be raised in the adoptive family with full legal status.

definitions.definition: 'adoption regulations' means the regulations framed by the Authority and notified by the Central Government in respect of adoption.
definitions.plain_english: Adoption regulations are the official rules made by the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) and published by the Central Government that govern how adoptions are carried out in India. These rules cover procedures, eligibility criteria, timelines, documentation, and other requirements that must be followed by all parties involved in an adoption — whether domestic or inter-country. They are legally binding and form the procedural backbone for all adoption processes under the Juvenile Justice Act.
real_world_examples: A couple in Mumbai wishes to adopt a child registered on the CARA portal; the adoption regulations specify the exact eligibility criteria, waiting periods, home study report requirements, and matching procedures they must follow before being considered for adoption.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Chennai places an orphan child with prospective adoptive parents; the adoption regulations govern how the agency must process the child's dossier, obtain the adoption order from the court, and maintain post-adoption follow-up records.

An NRI couple settled in Canada seeks to adopt an Indian child; the adoption regulations outline the specific documentation, no-objection certificate requirements, and inter-country adoption procedures they must comply with under CARA's framework.

A District Magistrate reviewing an adoption order under Section 60 of the Juvenile Justice Act must verify that all procedural requirements mandated by the adoption regulations — including home study reports, matching criteria, and waiting periods — have been duly complied with before passing the order.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Kolkata is inspected by CARA officials who check whether the agency is following the adoption regulations in terms of maintaining child registers, conducting background checks on prospective parents, and filing mandatory reports within prescribed timelines.
what_it_covers: Regulations specifying eligibility criteria and documentation requirements for prospective adoptive parents seeking to adopt under the Juvenile Justice Act framework.

Procedures governing the registration, matching, placement, and legal finalisation of adoptions including domestic, inter-State, and inter-country adoptions notified by the Central Government on CARA's recommendation.

Rules relating to timelines for adoption processes, post-adoption follow-up requirements, and the conduct and obligations of Specialised Adoption Agencies and other stakeholders involved in the adoption chain.
Provisions governing the handling of children legally free for adoption, including their registration on the Child Adoption Resource Information and Guidance System (CARINGS) maintained by CARA.
what_it_excludes: Informal or customary adoption arrangements (e.g., traditional adoptions under personal laws such as the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956) that fall outside the Juvenile Justice Act framework and are not governed by CARA-framed regulations.
General child welfare policies, institutional care guidelines, or aftercare regulations that are framed under other provisions of the Act and do not specifically pertain to the adoption process.

Regulations or rules framed by State Governments or State Adoption Resource Agencies independently, which do not constitute 'adoption regulations' unless framed by the Authority (CARA) and notified by the Central Government.
Court procedures and judicial orders relating to adoption, which are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure or relevant court rules rather than by the adoption regulations themselves.
definitions.why_it_matters: Compliance with adoption regulations is a mandatory legal prerequisite under Sections 57, 60, and 64 of the Juvenile Justice Act; any adoption proceeding, order, or agency function that deviates from these regulations is legally invalid and may expose agencies, prospective parents, or officials to penalties. The definition determines which regulatory framework applies to an adoption transaction, thereby triggering or blocking obligations related to eligibility, documentation, court orders, and post-adoption follow-up.

definitions.plain_english: Adoptive parents are people who have legally adopted a child and have taken on all the responsibilities of being that child's parent — just as if they were the biological mother and father. Once adoption is complete, the child belongs to them fully in the eyes of the law. They have the same duties toward the child as any birth parent would, including care, protection, and support.
real_world_examples: A married couple in Pune completes the CARA adoption process and legally adopts a three-year-old girl from a Specialised Adoption Agency; they are thereafter her adoptive parents under the Juvenile Justice Act.

A non-resident Indian (NRI) couple living in the United States adopts a child from an orphanage in Chennai through the inter-country adoption process; upon the issuance of an adoption order by the Indian court, they become the child's adoptive parents.
A widow in Delhi adopts a six-year-old abandoned boy who was declared legally free for adoption by the Child Welfare Committee; she becomes his sole adoptive parent with full legal parental rights.

A couple in Mumbai who had previously adopted a child is reported to have deserted that child; the Child Welfare Committee declares the child 'abandoned' based on desertion by the adoptive parents, triggering protective proceedings under the Act.

A child adopted by a couple in Kolkata through a registered adoption agency is subsequently found to be living on the street; an inquiry under Section 63 examines whether the adoptive parents have fulfilled their obligations under the adoption order.
what_it_covers: A married Indian couple who has received a court-issued adoption order through the CARA-regulated process and has taken custody of the adopted child.
A single individual who has lawfully adopted a child in accordance with the adoption regulations and has assumed full parental responsibility.
NRI or overseas citizen of India couples who have completed inter-country adoption proceedings and received recognition as legal parents of the child under Indian law.
Persons who adopted a child under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 or any other applicable personal law, where the adoption is legally recognised.
what_it_excludes: Foster parents or fit persons who are providing temporary care to a child but have not completed a legal adoption process.
Biological parents who gave birth to the child, even if they are currently the primary caregivers.
Guardians appointed by a court or Child Welfare Committee who have legal custody but have not adopted the child.
Prospective adoptive parents who are registered with CARA and awaiting a match but have not yet received an adoption order.
Relatives or kin caregivers providing informal care without completing a formal legal adoption procedure.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'adoptive parent' determines their full legal parental obligations under Section 63 and the Act — including liability for abandonment or neglect of the adopted child, which can trigger a Child Welfare Committee inquiry and protective proceedings. Desertion of a child by adoptive parents, as opposed to a mere guardian, directly activates the 'abandoned child' definition and consequent State intervention measures.

definitions.definition: After care refers to the support, including financial support, provided to any child leaving a child care institution upon completion of eighteen years of age, to facilitate such child's re-integration into the mainstream of society, in the manner as may be prescribed; and includes after care support obtainable under section 46, as well as Foster Care and Sponsorship After Care arrangements ordered by the Committee.
definitions.plain_english: After care is the help given to young people who are leaving government-run children's homes or other child care institutions when they turn 18. It can include money, housing support, and other assistance to help them live independently and become part of mainstream society. The government may also provide after care through foster care or sponsorship arrangements. Appeals about after care decisions go to the District Magistrate rather than the Children's Court.
real_world_examples: A 18-year-old girl who grew up in a Children's Home in Pune is provided a one-time financial grant and vocational training support under an after care programme to help her rent accommodation and secure employment as a seamstress after leaving the institution.

A boy who aged out of a child care institution in Delhi at 18 is placed under a sponsored after care arrangement where a government-approved NGO pays for his college hostel fees and monthly living expenses so he can complete his graduation.

A young man from a special home in Chennai, having completed 18 years, is connected with a skill development centre under the after care scheme and given a monthly stipend for six months while he undergoes a certified electrician training course.

A Child Welfare Committee in Kolkata passes an order directing that a child nearing 18 years in a fit facility receive after care support under section 46, including counselling services and assistance in obtaining documents such as an Aadhaar card and bank account to enable financial independence.

A girl leaving a Specialised Adoption Agency in Mumbai at 18 who could not be adopted challenges a denial of after care benefits before the District Magistrate, as appeals on after care matters lie with the District Magistrate under section 101 rather than the Children's Court.
semantic_tags: foster care and sponsorship after care
what_it_covers: Financial support provided to a child who has completed 18 years of age upon leaving a child care institution, to facilitate re-integration into mainstream society.
Foster Care After Care arrangements ordered by the Child Welfare Committee enabling a young adult who has aged out of institutional care to continue living with a foster family.
Sponsorship After Care orders made by the Committee to provide ongoing monetary or material support to an 18-year-old who has left a child care institution.
Appeals related to decisions on Foster Care and Sponsorship After Care, which lie specifically before the District Magistrate under section 101.
Orders passed by the Committee directing after care support under section 46 as part of rehabilitation and social re-integration planning for children nearing the age of majority.
what_it_excludes: Support or services provided to children who are still below 18 years of age and remain within a child care institution, as after care specifically applies upon completion of 18 years.
Children who leave child care institutions voluntarily or are restored to their families before turning 18, as the statutory trigger for after care is completion of 18 years of age.
Adoption-related financial or rehabilitative support, which is governed separately under adoption provisions and does not constitute after care under section 46.
Ongoing institutional care or residential placement within a child care institution after the age of 18, which is distinct from the transitional after care support envisaged by the Act.

Support provided to adult offenders or persons who were never placed in a child care institution under the Juvenile Justice Act, as after care is exclusive to children who have been housed in such institutions.

Failure to provide mandated after care support may constitute a breach of the prescribed statutory obligation of the concerned institution or government authority.

definitions.definition: 'Aftercare' means making provision of support, financial or otherwise, to persons, who have completed the age of eighteen years but have not completed the age of twenty-one years, and have left any institutional care to join the mainstream of the society.
definitions.plain_english: Aftercare refers to the support — which can be money, housing, vocational training, or other assistance — given to young adults between 18 and 21 years of age who have recently left a government or approved shelter or care home. The goal is to help them settle into normal life outside institutional care. It bridges the gap between leaving a child care facility and becoming fully independent.
real_world_examples: A 19-year-old boy who spent his teenage years in a Special Home in Mumbai after being found in conflict with law is provided monthly financial assistance and enrolled in a skill development programme under aftercare to help him find employment and stable housing.

An 18-year-old girl who lived in a Children's Home in Chennai after being rescued from child trafficking is given aftercare support in the form of a hostel facility and vocational training in tailoring until she turns 21.
A 20-year-old orphan who grew up in a registered children's home in Lucknow is provided aftercare counselling, a stipend, and assistance in opening a bank account to transition to independent living.

A young adult of 19 years who left an Observation Home in Kolkata after completing a rehabilitation programme receives aftercare in the form of educational sponsorship to continue college studies and periodic follow-up by the District Child Protection Unit.

An 18-year-old surrendered child who was placed in a Specialised Adoption Agency but was not adopted receives aftercare financial support and placement guidance from the State Government to help integrate into society after leaving institutional care.
what_it_covers: Financial assistance such as stipends, grants, or allowances provided to individuals aged 18 to 21 who have left institutional care.
Non-financial support including vocational training, educational sponsorship, counselling, housing, and employment guidance for former residents of child care institutions.

Young adults who have exited any recognised institutional care facility — such as Children's Homes, Special Homes, Observation Homes, or Specialised Adoption Agencies — and are attempting to reintegrate into mainstream society.
Periodic follow-up and monitoring by authorities to ensure that the person receiving aftercare is progressing toward independence.
what_it_excludes: Persons who are still below 18 years of age, as they remain under the active care and protection framework of the Act and are not yet eligible for aftercare.
Persons who have completed 21 years of age, since the definition explicitly caps eligibility at the age of twenty-one years.

Individuals who have not passed through any institutional care facility, such as children raised by biological or adoptive families throughout their childhood, even if they face financial hardship after turning 18.
General social welfare schemes or poverty alleviation programmes provided by the State to the adult population at large, which are not specifically directed at former institutional care residents.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'aftercare' triggers the State Government's obligation under the Act to frame and implement aftercare programmes specifically for this age group, and determines which young adults are legally entitled to access such support. Without satisfying this definition — particularly the requirements of age (18–21) and prior institutional care — a person cannot claim entitlement to aftercare services under the Juvenile Justice framework.

definitions.definition: "authorised foreign adoption agency" means a foreign social or child welfare agency that is authorised by the Central Adoption Resource Authority on the recommendation of their Central Authority or Government department of that country for sponsoring the application of non-resident Indian or overseas citizen of India or persons of Indian origin or foreign prospective adoptive parents for adoption of a child from India.
definitions.plain_english: An authorised foreign adoption agency is an overseas organisation that deals with child welfare and has been officially approved by India's Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) to help foreign nationals or Indian-origin persons living abroad adopt children from India. The approval comes after the agency's own government or a recognised authority in that country recommends it. Only through such an approved agency can prospective adoptive parents living outside India formally apply to adopt an Indian child.
real_world_examples: A US-based non-profit child welfare organisation, recommended by the US Department of State (acting as the Central Authority under the Hague Convention), receives CARA authorisation and begins sponsoring adoption applications of American couples wishing to adopt an Indian child.

A UK-based adoption agency recommended by the UK Central Authority for Inter-Country Adoption is authorised by CARA and assists a Non-Resident Indian couple settled in London in filing their application to adopt a child from a Specialised Adoption Agency in Maharashtra.

A German child welfare society, after receiving a recommendation from the German Central Authority (Bundeszentralstelle für Auslandsadoption), obtains CARA authorisation and sponsors the adoption application of a German couple seeking to adopt an infant from Tamil Nadu.

An Overseas Citizen of India living in Canada approaches a Canadian child welfare agency that holds CARA authorisation; the agency sponsors their home study report and application for adopting a special-needs child from a Children's Home in Rajasthan.

A person of Indian origin residing in Australia works through a CARA-authorised Australian adoption agency, which coordinates with the State Adoption Resource Agency in Karnataka to facilitate the inter-country adoption of an orphaned child declared legally free for adoption.
what_it_covers: A foreign social or child welfare agency located outside India that has been formally recommended by its country's Central Authority or Government department and subsequently authorised by CARA.

Agencies sponsoring adoption applications of non-resident Indians (NRIs), overseas citizens of India (OCIs), and persons of Indian origin (PIOs) who reside abroad and wish to adopt a child from India.

Agencies sponsoring adoption applications of foreign nationals (prospective adoptive parents who are neither NRI nor OCI nor of Indian origin) seeking to adopt an Indian child through the inter-country adoption process.

Foreign agencies operating in countries that are signatories to the Hague Convention on Inter-Country Adoption and whose government departments act as the recommending authority where a formal Central Authority exists.
what_it_excludes: Indian domestic adoption agencies or Specialised Adoption Agencies registered within India, which operate under a separate framework and are not classified as authorised foreign adoption agencies.

Foreign organisations that work in child welfare but have not received a recommendation from their country's Central Authority or Government department and have not been authorised by CARA — such agencies cannot legally sponsor inter-country adoption applications.

Private individuals or facilitators, whether Indian or foreign, acting independently without institutional recognition — individual facilitators are not agencies and cannot qualify under this definition.
Foreign agencies authorised only for domestic adoption within their own country and not specifically authorised by CARA for sponsoring adoptions from India.
Non-governmental organisations or foreign bodies engaged in child welfare activities in India (such as running shelters or schools) but not involved in sponsoring inter-country adoption applications.
definitions.why_it_matters: Only an authorised foreign adoption agency can legally sponsor and process inter-country adoption applications under Sections 59, 62, and 70 of the Juvenile Justice Act; applications sponsored by an unauthorised foreign entity are invalid and CARA cannot process them, making the entire adoption legally void. The authorisation status of the agency directly determines whether inter-country adoption proceedings can commence, and any violation of this requirement may expose parties to criminal liability under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Authority' means the Central Adoption Resource Authority constituted under section 68.
definitions.plain_english: The 'Authority' refers to the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), which is the apex body set up by the Central Government to oversee and regulate all adoption-related matters in India. It is responsible for framing adoption regulations, maintaining databases of children available for adoption, and coordinating both domestic and inter-country adoptions. Think of it as the national headquarters that governs how children in India are adopted legally and safely.
real_world_examples: A couple in Mumbai applies to adopt a child through a Specialised Adoption Agency — the Authority (CARA) maintains the central registry on its CARINGS portal and must ultimately approve the matching process.

A foreign prospective adoptive parent from the United States wishes to adopt an Indian child — the Authority issues the no-objection certificate and coordinates with the authorised foreign adoption agency and the relevant Central Authority of the receiving country.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Chennai is found to be violating adoption norms — the Authority has the power to suspend or cancel its recognition and initiate regulatory action under the adoption regulations it has framed.

A non-resident Indian couple settled in Dubai wants to adopt a child from India — the Authority processes and oversees their application, verifies the home study report, and facilitates the legal process in coordination with Indian diplomatic missions abroad.

A child declared legally free for adoption by a Child Welfare Committee in Kolkata is placed in the national adoption pool — the Authority's CARINGS database lists the child and matches prospective adoptive parents based on seniority and eligibility criteria.
what_it_covers: The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) constituted under section 68 of the Juvenile Justice Act, functioning as the apex body for adoption in India.
Framing and notifying adoption regulations in consultation with the Central Government, governing both in-country and inter-country adoptions.
Maintaining and administering the Child Adoption Resource Information and Guidance System (CARINGS) for matching children with prospective adoptive parents.
Granting recognition to Specialised Adoption Agencies and authorising foreign adoption agencies to sponsor applications for inter-country adoption.
Issuing no-objection certificates for inter-country adoptions and coordinating with Central Authorities of receiving countries under the Hague Convention.
what_it_excludes: State-level child protection bodies or State Adoption Resource Agencies, which are distinct entities operating at the state level and not equivalent to the Authority.
Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards, which are adjudicatory and inquiry bodies not vested with adoption regulatory functions.
District Child Protection Units, which are administrative units at the district level and do not constitute or replace the Authority.
Voluntary or non-governmental organisations operating as adoption agencies, even if recognised by the Authority — they are not the Authority itself.
The Central Authority under the Hague Convention, which is a separate recognised government department and is defined distinctly from the Authority under section 2 of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Sections 56 through 73 of the Act vest specific regulatory, administrative, and quasi-judicial powers exclusively in the Authority, meaning that adoption orders, agency recognitions, and inter-country adoption approvals are legally valid only when issued or sanctioned by the Authority. Any adoption process that bypasses or fails to involve the Authority as mandated renders the adoption legally defective and may attract penal consequences under the Act.

definitions.definition: An offence under the Juvenile Justice Act is bailable where it is punishable with imprisonment for less than three years or with fine only, in which case the accused has a right to be released on bail as a matter of course. It means the accused does not have to wait for a judge to decide whether bail will be granted; it is granted automatically upon request with or without a surety.
real_world_examples: A manager of a children's home in Maharashtra is accused of a minor record-keeping violation under the JJ Act punishable by a fine only — the police must release him on bail as a matter of right at the police station itself.

A social worker in Delhi is booked for a procedural breach under the JJ Act carrying a maximum sentence of two years — since the offence is bailable, she can walk out of the police station on bail without needing to approach a magistrate.

A registered adoption agency official in Chennai is arrested for a technical non-compliance that attracts imprisonment of up to one year — being a bailable offence, the official's lawyer can secure bail at the police station level without a court hearing.

A fit person in Kolkata caring for a child in need of care and protection is charged with a minor violation of conditions punishable with a fine — being bailable and non-cognizable, police cannot even arrest without a magistrate's order, and bail is a right if arrested.

A probation officer in Bengaluru is accused of negligently failing to submit a mandatory report, attracting less than three years' imprisonment under the JJ Act — the offence being bailable means the officer is entitled to bail as soon as he presents himself before the authorities.

definitions.definition: "Begging" means— (i) soliciting or receiving alms in a public place or entering into any private premises for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms, under any pretence; (ii) exposing or exhibiting with the object of obtaining or extorting alms, any sore, wound, injury, deformity or disease, whether of himself or of any other person or of an animal.
definitions.plain_english: Begging means asking for or accepting money or charity in a public place, or going into someone's home or private property to do so, under any excuse or pretext. It also includes deliberately showing off a physical wound, illness, disability, or deformity — whether one's own, another person's, or even an animal's — in order to get money or force people to give money. The law treats both voluntary and coerced forms of this conduct as begging.
real_world_examples: A child standing at a busy traffic signal in Mumbai holding out a hand to ask motorists for coins or food is engaged in begging under this definition.

An adult using a young child to display the child's visible physical injury or disability on a railway platform in Delhi to solicit money from passengers falls squarely within the second limb of the definition.

A group of children going door-to-door in a residential colony in Chennai claiming to collect donations for a festival, when their actual purpose is to receive alms for personal sustenance, constitutes entering private premises for soliciting alms.

A person sitting outside a temple in Varanasi with a deliberately exposed wound or sore on their body, positioned so that passers-by are prompted out of pity or fear to give money, constitutes begging by exhibition of injury.

A child forced by traffickers in Kolkata to carry a sick animal and parade it in a market area to extort money from shopkeepers is covered under the limb dealing with exhibition of an animal's disease or deformity.

A child in Hyderabad who approaches customers outside a shopping mall, under the pretence of selling small items but primarily soliciting charity, may be found to be begging under the pretence clause of the definition.

Receiving alms in a public place, even without active solicitation, if the act is part of a pattern of begging conduct.
what_it_excludes: Genuine organised charity collection drives conducted by registered non-governmental organisations with proper authorisation, where the purpose is institutional fundraising rather than personal alms.
A child selling goods or performing street arts such as juggling or music for a fee, where the primary purpose is commercial exchange of a service rather than soliciting charity.
Medical or welfare workers visiting private premises to provide assistance or assess need — there is no intent to solicit or receive alms in such visits.
A person legitimately seeking emergency help (such as asking for water or directions) from a private residence, where there is no intent to solicit money or material charity.

Religious mendicants or ascetics whose recognised spiritual tradition involves acceptance of food offerings in temples or ashrams, where the context is devotional rather than alms-seeking on a public street, may fall outside the practical scope of enforcement depending on context.

definitions.definition: 'Best interest of child' means the basis for any decision taken regarding the child, to ensure fulfilment of his basic rights and needs, identity, social well-being and physical, emotional and intellectual development.
definitions.plain_english: The 'best interest of the child' means that whenever any decision is made about a child — whether by a court, a committee, or any authority — the primary concern must be what is genuinely good for that child's overall health, happiness, identity, and growth. It is not just about immediate safety but also about the child's long-term emotional, social, and intellectual development. In simple terms, every decision must put the child's welfare first, above all other considerations.
real_world_examples: A Juvenile Justice Board in Mumbai is deciding whether to send a 14-year-old boy who committed a petty theft back to his abusive family or to a fit person's care. The Board applies the 'best interest' principle to determine that placement with a trained foster family better supports the child's emotional recovery and schooling.

A Child Welfare Committee in Delhi is evaluating an orphaned girl for adoption. Two prospective adoptive families are available — one wealthy but frequently travelling abroad and one middle-class but highly stable and engaged. Applying best interest, the Committee chooses the family that can provide consistent emotional and educational support.

A magistrate in Chennai is hearing a case where a child labourer rescued from a carpet factory needs rehabilitation. Relying on the best interest standard under Section 3, the magistrate directs that the child be enrolled in a residential school with counselling rather than returned to the village where economic pressure may push the child back into labour.

A State Government in Rajasthan is framing rules for aftercare of 18-to-21-year-olds leaving child care institutions. Using the best interest principle, the policy mandates vocational training, mental health support, and transitional housing to ensure these young adults can successfully integrate into society.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Kolkata is considering an inter-country adoption application for a surrendered child. The agency applies the best interest standard to determine whether in-country adoption options have been genuinely exhausted before allowing the child to be placed abroad, ensuring the child retains cultural and linguistic identity wherever possible.

definitions.definition: "Best interest of child" means the basis for any decision taken regarding the child, to ensure fulfilment of his basic rights and needs, identity, social well-being and physical, emotional and intellectual development.
definitions.plain_english: The 'best interest of the child' is the guiding principle that every decision made about a child must prioritise what is genuinely good for that child — covering their basic needs, identity, emotional health, and overall development. It means that when authorities, courts, or officials make choices affecting a child, the child's welfare comes first, above all other considerations. This standard applies in situations ranging from custody decisions to adoption, rehabilitation, and placement in care institutions.
real_world_examples: A Juvenile Justice Board in Mumbai is deciding whether to send a 15-year-old first-time offender to a special home or release them into community care; the Board applies the best interest standard to choose the option most likely to support the child's rehabilitation and emotional development.

A Child Welfare Committee in Delhi is determining whether an abandoned infant should be placed in a Children's Home or with a foster family; they weigh which arrangement better fulfils the child's need for identity, stability, and emotional bonding.

A family court in Chennai adjudicating custody of a 10-year-old between separated parents uses the best interest principle to assess which parent can better provide for the child's physical safety, education, and psychological well-being.

A District Magistrate in Rajasthan reviewing an adoption application under Section 96 evaluates whether the prospective adoptive parents' home environment, financial stability, and emotional readiness truly serve the best interest of the child being placed with them.

A Child Welfare Committee in Kolkata deciding whether to restore a child in need of care and protection to their biological parents — who have a history of neglect — applies the best interest standard to determine if restoration is safe or if alternative care is preferable.

An observation home superintendent in Hyderabad developing an individual care plan for a child in conflict with law ensures that educational, vocational, and counselling components are designed around the child's best interest rather than purely punitive goals.
what_it_covers: Decisions by the Juvenile Justice Board on placement, release, or rehabilitation of a child in conflict with law, where the child's emotional and intellectual development must be the primary consideration.
Determinations by the Child Welfare Committee on adoption, foster care, restoration, or institutional placement of a child in need of care and protection.
Individual care plans formulated for children in institutional care, ensuring their basic rights, identity, and developmental needs are addressed.
Evaluation of prospective adoptive parents' suitability under Section 96 and related provisions, where the child's social well-being and future development are central to approval.
Assessments by courts or authorities when deciding custody, guardianship, or any intervention affecting a child's physical, emotional, or intellectual growth.
what_it_excludes: Decisions made solely on administrative convenience or institutional resource constraints, without reference to the individual child's welfare, rights, or developmental needs.
The interests or preferences of parents, guardians, or prospective adoptive parents when these conflict with the child's own welfare, safety, and development.
Adult offenders (persons who have completed eighteen years of age) whose cases are governed by ordinary criminal law rather than the child-centric best interest standard.
Purely punitive or retributive approaches to a child in conflict with law that prioritise societal punishment over the child's rehabilitation and reintegration.
Financial or economic interests of the biological family or institution that override the child's need for a stable identity, safe environment, and emotional well-being.
definitions.why_it_matters: Every decision made under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act — including placement, adoption, restoration, individual care planning, and orders under Section 96 — is legally required to be grounded in the best interest of the child; failure to apply this standard can render an order legally unsound or subject to challenge. It operationally determines which placement, care arrangement, or legal action authorities must choose, and directly triggers or constrains the obligations of the Board, the Committee, courts, and all functionaries acting under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Board' means a Juvenile Justice Board constituted under section 4.
definitions.plain_english: The Board, formally called the Juvenile Justice Board, is a special legal body set up in each district to handle cases involving children who are accused of committing crimes. It is made up of a magistrate and social workers who together decide what happens to a child in conflict with the law. Instead of treating such children like adult criminals, the Board focuses on their rehabilitation and best interests.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy in Pune is arrested for allegedly snatching a mobile phone. The police present him before the Juvenile Justice Board in Pune district, which conducts an inquiry, orders a social investigation report, and decides to place him in an observation home pending final orders.

In Delhi, a 17-year-old is accused of participating in a gang-related assault. The Board assesses whether the offence falls under heinous, serious, or petty category, and in the case of a heinous offence, may conduct a preliminary assessment to determine if the child should be tried as an adult.

A 13-year-old girl in Chennai found begging on streets is brought before the Board, which determines she qualifies as a child in need of care and protection and transfers her case to the Child Welfare Committee for appropriate rehabilitation.

In Jaipur, a 16-year-old is produced before the Board after being caught in possession of a small quantity of narcotic drugs. The Board grants bail with conditions, orders counselling, and sets a date for further inquiry under the Juvenile Justice Act.

A child alleged to have committed a petty offence in a rural district of Madhya Pradesh is brought before the Board, which after inquiry decides to release the child on probation under the supervision of a probation officer, avoiding any punitive detention.
semantic_tags: child in conflict with law tribunal
what_it_covers: Cases involving any child alleged or found to have committed an offence who has not completed eighteen years of age on the date of commission of the offence.
Proceedings for preliminary assessment of a child accused of a heinous offence to determine whether they should be tried as an adult by the Children's Court.
Decisions relating to bail, placement in observation homes, social investigation reports, individual care plans, and final disposal orders for children in conflict with the law.
Transfer of cases to the Child Welfare Committee when a child in conflict with the law is also found to be a child in need of care and protection.
Inquiries into the age of a child alleged to be in conflict with the law when age is disputed during proceedings.
what_it_excludes: The Child Welfare Committee, which is a separate statutory body that handles children in need of care and protection and has no jurisdiction over children in conflict with the law.

Adult criminal courts such as Sessions Courts or Magistrate Courts, which have no jurisdiction to try offences committed by a person who was under eighteen years of age at the time of the offence (except where the Board refers a heinous offence case to the Children's Court).
The Children's Court, which is a distinct forum that handles heinous offence trials of children referred by the Board after a preliminary assessment.
Administrative or executive bodies such as the District Child Protection Unit or State Government departments, which do not perform adjudicatory functions over children in conflict with the law.
Proceedings concerning adoption, foster care, or child welfare placements unrelated to an offence, which fall under the jurisdiction of the Committee or designated adoption authorities.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether the Board has jurisdiction determines the entire procedural framework applicable to a child accused of an offence — including the right to bail, the nature of inquiry, the type of institutional placement, and the final disposition order; without the Board's involvement, no valid inquiry, detention, or rehabilitation order can be made against a child in conflict with the law. The Board's classification of an offence as petty, serious, or heinous directly triggers different legal consequences, including the possibility of the child being tried as an adult.

definitions.definition: Bondage, as used in Section 79 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, refers to a condition in which a child who is ostensibly engaged for employment is kept under restraint, control, or obligation such that their freedom is curtailed, their earnings are withheld, or such earnings are appropriated by another person for that person's own purposes. It encompasses any arrangement by which a child's labour is exploited through coercion, deception, or economic dependency in connection with employment, including selling goods, services, or entertainment in public places for economic gain.
definitions.plain_english: Bondage means keeping a child trapped in a work situation where they cannot freely leave, do not receive their own wages, or have their money taken away by the person who employs or controls them. It is a form of exploitation where a child is forced to work under conditions of control or confinement. Even if the arrangement looks like a normal job on the surface, it counts as bondage if the child is effectively not free.
real_world_examples: A dhaba owner in Uttar Pradesh recruits a 12-year-old boy from a poor village, promising wages but then retaining all his earnings claiming repayment of a 'loan' given to the child's family, effectively trapping the child in unpaid labour for months.

A domestic employer in Mumbai keeps a 14-year-old girl from Jharkhand as a household worker, confiscates her identity documents, locks her inside the house, and sends her salary directly to a placement agent, preventing her from leaving or accessing her own money.

A beedi factory in Tamil Nadu recruits children under the guise of apprenticeships, deducts money for housing and food costs to ensure the children always owe money and cannot leave without settling a fabricated debt.

A man in Delhi uses three children to sell balloons and small toys at traffic signals, collects all their daily earnings at the end of the day, provides them minimal food, and threatens punishment if they return without meeting a daily target, keeping them in a state of economic bondage.

A rag-picking gang operator in Kolkata controls a group of orphaned children by housing them in a locked shed, taking all proceeds from their collection of recyclables, and using the money for his own business while providing only bare subsistence to the children.
what_it_covers: A situation where a child is engaged for work but physically or economically prevented from leaving the employment arrangement.
Cases where an employer, contractor, or any person withholds wages earned by a child and uses those earnings for their own financial benefit.
Arrangements where children are made to sell goods, services, or perform entertainment in public places and the proceeds are taken away from them by someone exercising control over them.
Debt bondage schemes where a child's labour is pledged to repay a loan advanced to the child or the child's family, keeping the child in perpetual obligation.
Situations of ostensible employment where the child has no practical freedom to leave due to threats, confinement, document confiscation, or other forms of coercion.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate employment or apprenticeship arrangements where a child above the permissible age receives their due wages freely and is not prevented from leaving the job.
Parental supervision of a child's minor earnings within a family context where no exploitative third party appropriates the earnings for their own commercial purposes.

Voluntary participation of a child in a school-organised or NGO-supervised activity involving economic skills training, where earnings if any are held in trust for the child's benefit and the child is free to discontinue.
Situations involving adults, since the provision specifically governs the exploitation of a 'child' as defined under the Juvenile Justice Act.
Cases of unpaid internships or educational placements sanctioned by law where there is no exploitative withholding of earnings, as no earnings arise to be withheld.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a situation qualifies as bondage under Section 79 determines whether the person exercising control over the child faces rigorous imprisonment of up to five years and a fine of one lakh rupees; establishing bondage also triggers the child's classification as a child in need of care and protection, activating the jurisdiction of the Child Welfare Committee and the child protection machinery under the Act.
