definitions.definition: A home study report is a document prepared by a Specialised Adoption Agency (in the case of domestic adoption) or an authorised foreign adoption agency, Central Authority, or concerned Government department (in the case of inter-country adoption) that assesses and evaluates the eligibility and suitability of prospective adoptive parents for adopting a child, in the manner as provided in the adoption regulations framed by the Authority.
definitions.plain_english: A home study report is an official document that checks whether a family or individual wanting to adopt a child is suitable and capable of raising that child. It is prepared by a recognised adoption agency or government body and looks at things like the family's background, finances, home environment, and emotional readiness. Only after this report confirms eligibility can the adoption process move forward officially.
real_world_examples: A couple from Mumbai applies to a Specialised Adoption Agency to adopt an orphan child; the agency visits their home, interviews them, reviews their financial records and health certificates, and prepares a home study report certifying their eligibility before referring a child to them.

A non-resident Indian couple living in the United States wishes to adopt an Indian child; the authorised foreign adoption agency in the USA conducts a detailed assessment of their household, employment, and parenting capacity, and submits the home study report to CARA along with their adoption application.

An overseas citizen of India residing in Canada applies through the Central Authority of Canada to adopt a child from India; the Central Authority prepares a home study report following Indian and Canadian adoption regulations before sponsoring their application to the Authority.

A single Indian woman living in Delhi applies to a Specialised Adoption Agency to adopt a girl child; the agency prepares a home study report assessing her income, living conditions, support network, and psychological readiness, which is then submitted to the District Magistrate as part of the adoption proceedings.

A foreign couple from Germany applies to adopt an Indian child with a physical disability; the concerned German Government department prepares a home study report evaluating their capacity to provide specialised care, which is then forwarded to CARA for further processing.
what_it_covers: Assessment of the financial stability, health, home environment, and background of Indian prospective adoptive parents living in India, prepared by a Specialised Adoption Agency.

Evaluation of non-resident Indians, overseas citizens of India, persons of Indian origin, or foreign nationals living abroad by an authorised foreign adoption agency, Central Authority, or concerned Government department for inter-country adoption eligibility.
Documentation of the social, psychological, and material readiness of a prospective adoptive family to raise an adopted child, as required under adoption regulations framed by CARA.
Assessment of a single prospective adoptive parent's suitability, including personal background, employment, and support systems, as part of the adoption application process.
what_it_excludes: The child study report, which is a separate document assessing the background, health, and needs of the child proposed for adoption rather than the adopting family.
The medical report of the child, which is independently prepared and distinct from the home study report of the prospective adoptive parents.
Post-adoption follow-up or progress reports submitted after the adoption order is passed, which track the child's wellbeing in the adoptive family rather than evaluating parental eligibility.

Assessments or background checks conducted informally or without the involvement of a Specialised Adoption Agency, authorised foreign adoption agency, Central Authority, or concerned Government department.
Surrender deeds or legal documents related to the relinquishment of a child, which concern the biological parent and are unrelated to the prospective adoptive parents' assessment.

definitions.definition: In-country adoption refers to the adoption of a child by prospective adoptive parents who are Indian citizens residing within India, where the entire adoption process is completed within the territorial jurisdiction of India, as distinct from inter-country adoption. The Central Adoption Resource Authority is mandated under Section 68 to promote in-country adoptions as a preferred and primary channel of adoption before considering inter-country placement.
definitions.plain_english: In-country adoption means when a child living in India is adopted by an Indian family also living in India, and the whole process happens within India itself. It is considered the first and preferred option before looking for adoptive parents abroad. definitions.definition: An 'individual care plan' is a comprehensive development plan for a child, prepared by the Probation Officer or Child Welfare Officer or case worker, as the case may be, in consultation with the child and their family, based on age and gender-specific needs, with the aim of ensuring the care, protection, restoration, treatment, rehabilitation, education, training, and reintegration of the child, and which forms part of the final order passed by the Board or the Committee for the child's rehabilitation and follow-up.
definitions.plain_english: An individual care plan is a personalised written plan made for each child who comes into contact with the juvenile justice system. It is created by a trained officer after talking to the child and their family, and sets out exactly what support, education, training, and care the child needs to get back on track. It acts as a roadmap guiding every authority — from the Board to welfare officers — on what steps to take for that specific child's rehabilitation and reintegration into society.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy from Delhi caught for petty theft is produced before the Juvenile Justice Board. The Probation Officer prepares an individual care plan recommending his enrollment in a vocational training programme for carpentry, regular counselling sessions, and monthly follow-up visits by the District Child Protection Unit to monitor his progress.

A 14-year-old girl rescued from a bonded labour situation in Tamil Nadu is brought before the Child Welfare Committee. A case worker prepares her individual care plan specifying restoration to her mother, bridge schooling to rejoin Class 8, trauma counselling, and sponsorship support for one year to cover school expenses.

A 17-year-old from Mumbai convicted of a serious offence and sent to a special home has an individual care plan drawn up that includes skill development in computer literacy, group therapy for anger management, legal literacy sessions, and a phased aftercare support plan upon release.

A child in conflict with law from a rural district in Rajasthan, found to be addicted to substances, has an individual care plan that mandates admission to an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts, family counselling, and a reintegration plan including enrollment in an open schooling programme post-treatment.

An orphan child in conflict with law in Kolkata, with no family support, has an individual care plan that includes placement in a children's home, identification of a fit person for eventual fostering, and a structured educational and vocational pathway reviewed every three months by the Management Committee of the institution.
what_it_covers: Personalised educational, vocational, and psychological intervention strategies tailored to the specific child's age, gender, and circumstances.
Plans for restoration, reintegration, and aftercare support including follow-up by the Probation Officer, District Child Protection Unit, or a non-governmental organisation.
Assessment of the child's family background, home environment, and specific needs prepared in consultation with the child and their family before or during inquiry proceedings.
Placement decisions such as recommending a special home, children's home, fit person, or foster care as part of the rehabilitation strategy.
Monitoring and review mechanisms specifying intervals and responsible authorities for follow-up on the child's progress post-order.
what_it_excludes: General institutional rules or standing orders applicable to all children in a child care institution, which are not tailored to an individual child.
The social investigation report prepared by the Probation Officer, which is an investigative input document and not itself the care plan.
Punitive or sentencing orders passed by the Board, such as fines or directions for community service, which are distinct from the rehabilitation plan embedded in the individual care plan.
Administrative plans or management policies of a child care institution that govern the institution as a whole rather than addressing the needs of a specific child.
Plans or orders relating solely to adults involved in proceedings, such as directions to parents to pay maintenance, which do not form part of the child's individual care plan.
definitions.why_it_matters: The individual care plan is a mandatory component of the final order passed by the Board or Committee and directly determines the nature, duration, and mode of a child's rehabilitation and reintegration; without it, the statutory obligation under sections 14, 39, and 53 to ensure the child's best interest in the disposal of the case remains unfulfilled. It triggers ongoing obligations on the Probation Officer, District Child Protection Unit, and child care institutions to implement, monitor, and review the prescribed interventions, making it a legally enforceable instrument for the child's welfare.

definitions.definition: "Inquiry" means a formal proceeding conducted by the Juvenile Justice Board or the Child Welfare Committee, as the case may be, to determine the status, circumstances, and appropriate course of action in respect of a child in conflict with law or a child in need of care and protection, in accordance with the procedure prescribed under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An inquiry is an official investigation or formal process carried out by the Juvenile Justice Board or the Child Welfare Committee to look into the background, situation, and needs of a child who has been brought before them. It helps the authority decide what is best for the child — whether the child needs protection, rehabilitation, or what action should be taken if the child is alleged to have committed an offence. The process is child-friendly and distinct from a regular criminal trial.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy in Mumbai is apprehended by police for allegedly stealing from a shop. The Juvenile Justice Board in Mumbai conducts an inquiry to understand his family background, school history, and circumstances of the offence before deciding on a suitable rehabilitation measure.

A 7-year-old girl found wandering alone at a railway station in Delhi is produced before the Child Welfare Committee, which initiates an inquiry to determine whether she is an abandoned child, ascertain her identity, trace her parents, and assess her need for care and protection.

A Child Welfare Committee in Chennai conducts an inquiry under Section 38 to determine whether a child whose parents have been missing for over two years is 'legally free for adoption', involving home visits, police verification, and documentation review.

In Kolkata, a 16-year-old alleged to have committed a heinous offence is brought before the Juvenile Justice Board, which conducts an inquiry including a social investigation report and psychological assessment to determine whether the child should be tried as an adult or treated as a juvenile.

A District Child Protection Unit in Jaipur refers a surrendered infant to the Child Welfare Committee, which undertakes a due inquiry process to verify the genuineness of the surrender deed and declare the child abandoned before placing the child in a Specialised Adoption Agency.
what_it_covers: Proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board to determine guilt, background, and appropriate disposition for a child alleged to be in conflict with law.
Proceedings before the Child Welfare Committee to assess whether a child qualifies as a child in need of care and protection, including verification of abandonment, surrender, or abuse.
Formal process to declare a child as 'legally free for adoption' after examining evidence of abandonment or unavailability of parents.
Social investigation and home background assessment conducted as part of determining individual care plans for children brought before the Board or Committee.
Inquiry conducted to assess whether a child who has committed a heinous offence should be tried as a child or referred to a Children's Court for trial as an adult.
what_it_excludes: Regular criminal trials or proceedings conducted against adults under the Code of Criminal Procedure, which are governed by a different statutory framework and not considered 'inquiry' under this Act.
Informal or preliminary checks by police at the field level before a child is formally produced before the Board or Committee, which do not constitute a statutory inquiry.
Administrative reviews or inspections of child care institutions by the inspection committee, which are oversight functions and not inquiries into a specific child's status.
Adoption home study reports prepared by recognised adoption agencies for prospective adoptive parents, which are evaluative processes distinct from the statutory inquiry into a child's status.
Investigations conducted by Child Welfare Police Officers solely for intelligence or law enforcement purposes that do not result in formal production before the Board or Committee.
definitions.why_it_matters: The conduct of a proper inquiry is a mandatory procedural safeguard that determines the legal status of a child — whether they are declared abandoned, in need of care, legally free for adoption, or subject to rehabilitation — and any failure to conduct due inquiry invalidates orders such as declarations of abandonment or fitness for adoption. It also governs whether a child in conflict with law receives juvenile justice measures or is referred to a Children's Court, directly impacting the child's liberty and future.

definitions.definition: An inspection committee is a body appointed by the State Government for the State and district, as the case may be, for all institutions registered or recognised to be fit under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2016, constituted for such period and for such purposes as may be prescribed, with the mandate to conduct mandatory periodic visits to all facilities housing children and submit inspection reports to the District Magistrate for further action.
definitions.plain_english: An inspection committee is an official group set up by the State Government to regularly check on all homes and institutions that house children under the Juvenile Justice Act. It must visit every such facility at least once every three months, with a team of at least three people including one woman and one doctor. After each visit, the committee writes a report and sends it to the District Magistrate within a week so that any problems can be fixed.
real_world_examples: The Maharashtra State Government constitutes a district-level inspection committee comprising a District Child Protection Officer, a female social worker, and a government medical officer, which visits a Children's Home in Pune every quarter to check hygiene, food quality, staff conduct, and child safety conditions.

An inspection committee appointed by the Government of Tamil Nadu visits an unregistered private shelter in Chennai that is reportedly housing street children, using its power under Section 41 to inspect even non-registered institutions to determine whether children in need of care and protection are being housed there.

A district inspection committee in Rajasthan conducts a surprise visit to a Special Home housing children in conflict with law in Jaipur, finds overcrowding and inadequate medical facilities, and submits a report to the District Magistrate within seven days, triggering a compliance order within the next month.

The State-level inspection committee in Karnataka reviews an Observation Home in Bengaluru after receiving complaints from a child rights NGO, documents violations of prescribed norms, and recommends to the District Magistrate that the institution's registration be reviewed and corrective measures be enforced.

A district inspection committee in Uttar Pradesh, during a mandatory quarterly visit to an open shelter in Lucknow, interviews children individually to check for signs of abuse or exploitation, and the woman member of the committee conducts a separate session with girl children to ensure their safety and well-being.
what_it_covers: State-level and district-level committees appointed by the State Government to inspect all registered or recognised child care institutions under the Juvenile Justice Act.

Mandatory visits to every facility housing children in the assigned area at least once in three months, conducted by a team of not less than three members including at least one woman and one medical officer.
Inspection of unregistered institutions housing children to determine whether such children are in need of care and protection, as empowered under Section 41.
Submission of written inspection reports to the District Magistrate within one week of each visit, detailing findings and recommending further action.
Follow-up compliance monitoring, as the District Magistrate must take action within one month of receiving the report and submit a compliance report to the State Government.
what_it_excludes: Judicial or quasi-judicial adjudicatory functions such as determining guilt or passing orders on individual children, which are the exclusive domain of the Juvenile Justice Board or the Child Welfare Committee.
Private residences, foster families, or individual guardians who are not running an institution or facility for housing multiple children under the Act.

Adoption agencies or processes governed purely under the Central Adoption Resource Authority regulations, which have separate oversight and audit mechanisms beyond the scope of Section 54 inspection committees.
Law enforcement or police investigation functions; the inspection committee has no power to arrest, detain, or initiate criminal proceedings against institution staff or management.
Administrative functions of the Child Welfare Committee or Juvenile Justice Board, such as conducting inquiries into individual cases or passing rehabilitation orders for specific children.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and functioning of an inspection committee is the primary safeguard mechanism that ensures child care institutions comply with prescribed standards under the Act; failure of an institution to permit inspection or failure of State Government to constitute such committees can trigger departmental action, cancellation or withholding of the institution's registration under Section 41, and State Government takeover of management. The committee's reports directly activate the District Magistrate's statutory obligation to take corrective action, making timely inspection reports a prerequisite for enforcing child protection norms across all housing facilities.

definitions.definition: "Institution" as used in Section 53 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 refers to any child care institution, observation home, special home, place of safety, Children's Home, or open shelter established, maintained, or recognised under this Act for the reception, care, rehabilitation, and reintegration of children in conflict with law or children in need of care and protection.
definitions.plain_english: An 'institution' under this law refers to any officially recognised facility or home set up to look after children who are either in trouble with the law or who need care and protection. These places provide shelter, food, education, and rehabilitation services to such children. They must be registered and are regularly inspected to ensure children are treated well and their rights are protected.
real_world_examples: A Government-run observation home in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh where children alleged to have committed offences are kept while their cases are being heard by the Juvenile Justice Board.
A special home in Mumbai managed by a registered NGO that houses children aged 14–18 who have been found guilty of serious offences and need structured rehabilitation and vocational training.
A Children's Home in Chennai run by the Tamil Nadu State Government where orphaned and abandoned girls are housed, educated, and prepared for eventual adoption or reintegration into society.
A place of safety in Delhi designated by the State Government to hold a child above the age of 16 who has been tried as an adult and is awaiting sentencing by the Children's Court.
An open shelter in Kolkata providing temporary accommodation and crisis intervention services to street children and runaways who are identified as children in need of care and protection.
what_it_covers: Observation homes established under Section 47 of the Act for keeping children alleged to be in conflict with law during the pendency of inquiry.
Special homes established under Section 48 for housing and reforming children found to be in conflict with law after adjudication by the Juvenile Justice Board.
Children's Homes established or maintained by State Governments under Section 50 for children in need of care and protection.
Places of safety designated under Section 49 for keeping children above 16 years who are being tried as adults or who need special protection.
Open shelters set up under Section 43 as community-based facilities providing residential care to children in difficult circumstances on a short-term basis.
Specialised Adoption Agencies recognised under Section 65 that also function as residential care institutions for children legally free for adoption.
what_it_excludes: Private households or foster families providing informal care to children, as these are not registered institutions under the Act.
Schools, hospitals, or general welfare centres that serve children incidentally but are not specifically established or registered under the Juvenile Justice Act.
Unauthorised or unregistered shelters or homes operating without recognition from the State Government, even if they house children in need.

definitions.definition: 'Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts' shall have the meaning assigned to it under the scheme called 'Central Sector Scheme of Assistance for Prevention of Alcoholism and Substance (Drugs) Abuse and for Social Defence Services' framed by the Central Government in the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment or any other corresponding scheme for the time being in force.
definitions.plain_english: An Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA) is a government-recognised facility that provides inpatient treatment and rehabilitation to individuals addicted to alcohol, narcotic drugs, or psychotropic substances. These centres are established and funded under a Central Government scheme run by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, children with addiction issues may be sent to such centres after initial psychiatric evaluation and on the recommendation of the discharging psychiatric hospital.
real_world_examples: A 16-year-old boy held in an observation home in Mumbai is found to be severely dependent on heroin. After being assessed at a government psychiatric hospital, the Juvenile Justice Board orders his transfer to an IRCA in Pune for a structured inpatient de-addiction programme for the minimum period required for his treatment.

A 14-year-old girl in a Children's Home in Delhi is discovered to be addicted to inhalants (whitener/correction fluid fumes). Following a psychiatric evaluation and certificate of discharge, the Child Welfare Committee directs her placement in a nearby IRCA under the Central Sector Scheme for de-addiction and counselling.

A street child aged 15 rescued in Chennai and placed in a special home is found to be addicted to cannabis and alcohol. The Board, acting on the psychiatric hospital's discharge advice, transfers him to an IRCA in Tamil Nadu maintained by the State Government for the duration of his inpatient rehabilitation.

A 17-year-old in conflict with law, lodged in a special home in Kolkata, is identified as being addicted to psychotropic substances. The Juvenile Justice Board, after receiving the discharge certificate from a psychiatric nursing home, orders his temporary removal to an IRCA affiliated with the Central Sector Scheme for comprehensive substance abuse treatment.

A surrendered child in a Specialised Adoption Agency in Hyderabad is found to exhibit severe behavioural changes due to alcohol dependence. The Child Welfare Committee, after psychiatric assessment, directs placement in a State Government-run IRCA for the period of inpatient treatment before the child is returned to institutional care.
what_it_covers: Centres recognised and funded under the 'Central Sector Scheme of Assistance for Prevention of Alcoholism and Substance (Drugs) Abuse and for Social Defence Services' by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.

Similar centres maintained by the State Government for mentally ill persons, including persons addicted to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, where a child may be placed for inpatient treatment.
Any corresponding or successor scheme notified by the Central Government that replaces or updates the original Central Sector Scheme, ensuring continuity of legal recognition for qualifying centres.

Inpatient treatment of children transferred from psychiatric hospitals or psychiatric nursing homes on the basis of a certificate of discharge, for the minimum period required for their rehabilitation.
what_it_excludes: General hospitals or private clinics that offer de-addiction services but are not recognised or affiliated under the Central Sector Scheme or a corresponding State Government scheme.

Psychiatric hospitals and psychiatric nursing homes, which are separately defined under the Mental Health Act, 1987, and serve the prior stage of clinical psychiatric assessment before a child may be referred to an IRCA.
Outpatient de-addiction or counselling programmes that do not provide structured inpatient treatment, as the Act specifies removal to an IRCA only for the period of inpatient treatment.
Non-governmental or voluntary organisation-run rehabilitation centres that have not been recognised or designated under the applicable Central or State Government scheme for substance abuse services.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether the Committee or Board has legal authority to transfer a child out of a juvenile justice institution and into a specialised rehabilitation facility for addiction treatment; placement in a centre that does not qualify as an IRCA under the prescribed scheme would render the transfer order legally invalid. It also limits the duration of such removal strictly to the period of inpatient treatment, protecting the child's rights against indefinite or arbitrary placement outside the juvenile justice framework.

definitions.definition: "inter country adoption" means adoption of a child from India by non-resident Indians, overseas citizens of India, persons of Indian origin, or foreign prospective adoptive parents, facilitated through the Central Adoption Resource Authority and governed by the Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Cooperation in Inter-country Adoption (1993), wherein the child is permanently placed with adoptive parents residing in a country other than India.
definitions.plain_english: Inter country adoption means adopting a child from India by parents who live in another country. This includes Indian-origin people settled abroad as well as foreign nationals who want to adopt an Indian child. The process is overseen by a central government body called CARA and follows an international treaty to protect children's rights during such adoptions.
real_world_examples: An Indian child declared legally free for adoption by a Child Welfare Committee in Maharashtra is adopted by a couple of Indian origin permanently residing in the United States, processed through CARA and an authorised foreign adoption agency in the US.

A French couple applies through the French Central Authority and an authorised foreign adoption agency to adopt an orphan child from a Specialised Adoption Agency in Tamil Nadu, completing the process under CARA's inter country adoption regulations.

A Non-Resident Indian couple holding OCI cards and living in Canada adopt an abandoned child from a registered Children's Home in Rajasthan, following the inter country adoption process mandated under the Juvenile Justice Act.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Delhi lists a child on the adoption portal who has remained unmatched for the prescribed period under in-country adoption; the child is subsequently considered for inter country adoption by a family of Indian origin residing in Australia.

A child surrendered by biological parents to a Child Welfare Committee in Kerala is eventually placed for inter country adoption with a German family after exhausting all in-country adoption possibilities, as facilitated by CARA under the Hague Convention framework.

what_it_excludes: In-country adoption, where both the child and the adoptive parents reside within India, regardless of the child's religion, caste, or background.
Inter-State adoption within India, where adoptive parents from one Indian state adopt a child from another Indian state through the domestic adoption process.
Informal or unregistered overseas placement of children by biological parents or relatives without following the CARA-mandated inter country adoption process.
Foster care or guardianship arrangements with families abroad that do not result in a legal, permanent adoption order recognised under Indian law.
Adoption of children by foreigners residing in India on temporary visas who do not meet the eligibility criteria for prospective adoptive parents under adoption regulations.

definitions.definition: Intestacy, as used in Section 63 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, refers to the legal condition of dying without a valid will, in which context an adopted child shall be treated as the natural-born child of the adoptive parents for all purposes of inheritance and succession upon their dying intestate, with effect from the date the adoption order takes effect.
definitions.plain_english: Intestacy means the situation where a person dies without leaving a valid will, and their property is then distributed according to the law of inheritance. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, once a child is legally adopted, that child is treated exactly like a biological child of the adoptive parents — including their right to inherit the adoptive parents' property if they die without a will. Similarly, the adopted child's biological family loses any claim over the child's inheritance under intestacy rules.
real_world_examples: Ramesh and Sunita adopt a girl child through a recognised adoption agency in Mumbai. Ramesh later dies without making a will. Under intestacy rules, the adopted daughter inherits an equal share of Ramesh's property alongside any biological children, exactly as if she had been born to Ramesh.

A couple in Chennai adopt a boy whose biological parents have surrendered him. When the adoptive mother dies intestate years later, the adopted son is entitled to claim her property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as the adoption order treats him as her natural son.

An orphan from a children's home in Delhi is adopted by a couple. The biological grandparents of the adoptive father die without a will. Since the adoption severs all ties with the birth family and creates new ones in the adoptive family, the adopted child may have inheritance rights through the adoptive lineage under applicable intestacy law.

A non-resident Indian couple adopts a child under the Juvenile Justice Act. The adoptive father, who owns property in both India and abroad, dies intestate. The adopted child is entitled to claim inheritance in the Indian estate on the same footing as a biological child, because the adoption order under Section 63 treats the child as born to the adoptive parents for all purposes including intestacy.

A surrendered child adopted by a family in Kolkata later predeceases the adoptive parents without leaving a will. The adoptive parents can claim the child's estate under intestacy rules, just as biological parents could, since the adoption order fully integrates the child into the adoptive family for succession purposes.
what_it_covers: The right of an adopted child to inherit the adoptive parents' property when they die without a valid will, on the same basis as a biological child.
The right of adoptive parents to inherit from the adopted child if the child dies intestate, as they are treated in law as the child's natural parents.

All succession and inheritance matters governed by personal law (such as the Hindu Succession Act, 1956) that arise in the absence of a will, to which the adopted child becomes a full party from the date the adoption order takes effect.
The exclusion of the biological family from any intestacy-based inheritance claim over the adopted child's property, as all legal ties with the birth family are severed by the adoption order.
what_it_excludes: Property that had already vested in the adopted child before the adoption order took effect — such pre-existing property continues to vest in the adopted child but does not fall under the adoptive family's intestacy claims retroactively.

Testamentary succession, i.e., inheritance governed by a valid will — intestacy only applies when there is no will, so the term does not cover situations where the deceased left a legally executed testament.

Obligations attached to pre-adoption property, such as duties to maintain biological family relatives — these continue independently and are not displaced by the adoption order or intestacy provisions.

Claims by the biological family under intestacy law over the adopted child's estate — once the adoption order takes effect, the birth family's legal ties are severed and they have no intestacy-based inheritance rights.
definitions.why_it_matters: The inclusion of intestacy in Section 63 determines that an adopted child acquires full and equal inheritance rights within the adoptive family under applicable succession laws, ensuring no discrimination between adopted and biological children in property distribution upon death without a will. It also legally extinguishes the biological family's intestacy-based claims, making the adoption order a complete civil transformation of the child's legal identity for succession purposes.

definitions.definition: Intoxicating liquor refers to any alcoholic beverage or spirituous liquid capable of causing intoxication when consumed, including country liquor, arrack, toddy, beer, wine, whisky, rum, and other fermented or distilled alcoholic preparations. Though not expressly defined in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, the term is used in Sections 77 and 78 to denote any liquor with intoxicating properties that is given to or used to implicate a child in its trade or distribution.
definitions.plain_english: Intoxicating liquor means any drink that contains alcohol and can make a person drunk or impair their senses. This includes everything from cheap locally brewed alcohol like arrack or toddy to packaged drinks like beer, wine, or whisky. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, it is illegal to give such drinks to children or to use children to sell, carry, or deliver them.
real_world_examples: A dhabha owner in rural Rajasthan sends a 12-year-old boy to deliver bottles of country liquor (desi sharab) to nearby households — this directly falls under Section 78 as using a child to supply intoxicating liquor.

An unlicensed arrack seller in Andhra Pradesh involves a 14-year-old girl in carrying pouches of arrack to customers during night hours to avoid police detection, constituting a punishable offence under Section 78.
A hotel manager in Mumbai instructs a 15-year-old child worker to serve beer and whisky to adult guests at the bar, amounting to using a child for vending intoxicating liquor.

A bootlegger operating during dry days in Gujarat uses multiple children aged 10–13 to smuggle and peddle illicit liquor (hooch) across ward boundaries, attracting rigorous imprisonment under Section 78.

During a wedding function in Delhi, an adult relative repeatedly offers and gives glasses of wine and beer to a 10-year-old child without any medical prescription, attracting liability under Section 77 of the Act.

A liquor shop owner in Bengaluru employs a 16-year-old as an informal assistant who regularly hands over sealed bottles of whisky to adult customers at the counter, constituting vending of intoxicating liquor through a child.
what_it_covers: Country liquor, arrack, toddy, mahua, and other locally brewed or distilled alcoholic beverages commonly found in Indian rural and semi-urban settings.
Packaged and branded alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine, whisky, rum, vodka, and brandy sold through licensed outlets.
Illicitly manufactured or smuggled alcohol (hooch) that is traded outside legal licensing channels and is still capable of causing intoxication.
Any fermented beverage with a significant alcohol content that impairs judgment or physical faculties when consumed, regardless of whether it is legally permitted or prohibited in a given State.
Liquor used as a medium through which children are exploited for vending, peddling, carrying, supplying, or smuggling activities under Section 78.
what_it_excludes: Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, which are separately enumerated alongside intoxicating liquor in Sections 77 and 78 and governed by distinct legislation such as the NDPS Act, 1985.
Tobacco products and tobacco-based substances, which are explicitly listed separately in Section 77 and are not classified as intoxicating liquor under the Act.
Medicinal or pharmaceutical alcohol-based preparations administered on the written order of a duly qualified medical practitioner, which are expressly exempted under Section 77.
Non-alcoholic beverages such as mocktails, fruit juices, soft drinks, or energy drinks that do not contain alcohol and cannot cause intoxication.
Alcohol-based sanitisers, perfumes, or industrial solvents not intended for consumption, even if they contain high alcohol content.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as intoxicating liquor determines whether an adult who gives it to a child, or uses a child to trade in it, commits a punishable offence under Sections 77 and 78 of the Juvenile Justice Act, attracting rigorous imprisonment of up to seven years and a fine of up to one lakh rupees. The classification directly triggers child protection obligations and criminal liability, distinguishing liquor-related offences from those involving narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances which may attract additional penalties under the NDPS Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'juvenile' is not separately defined in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; however, based on the Act's framework and consistent usage, a juvenile refers to a person who has not completed eighteen years of age and is alleged or found to have committed an offence, thereby falling within the category of a child in conflict with law under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A juvenile is simply a young person — a child below 18 years of age — who is suspected of or has committed a crime. Instead of being treated like an adult criminal, the law gives them special protection and a different process focused on reform and rehabilitation. The system recognises that children may commit offences due to circumstances beyond their full control and should be given a chance to correct their behaviour.
real_world_examples: A 16-year-old boy from Delhi is caught by police for snatching a mobile phone. Since he is below 18, he is treated as a juvenile and produced before the Juvenile Justice Board rather than a regular criminal court.

A 15-year-old girl in Mumbai is found involved in a petty theft case at a local market. She is classified as a juvenile and instead of being sent to jail, she is sent to an observation home pending inquiry by the Board.

A 17-year-old from Chennai is accused of participating in a gang fight resulting in grievous hurt. Because the offence is classified as heinous, the Juvenile Justice Board assesses whether he should be tried as an adult, but he still enters the system as a juvenile.

A 14-year-old in Kolkata is apprehended for alleged involvement in drug peddling. As a juvenile, he cannot be sentenced to imprisonment in an adult prison; the Board determines appropriate rehabilitation measures under the Act.

A 13-year-old tribal boy in Jharkhand is accused of damaging government property during an agitation. Being below 18, he is handled exclusively under the juvenile justice system, ensuring age-appropriate care and legal procedures.
what_it_covers: A person below 18 years of age on the date of commission of an alleged offence who is apprehended by police or produced before the Juvenile Justice Board.
A child who is alleged to have committed a petty, serious, or heinous offence and is undergoing inquiry or trial under the juvenile justice system.
A child who has been detained, apprehended, or is in conflict with law and for whom decisions about observation homes, rehabilitation, or placement in a special home are being made by the Board.
A person below 18 years found in a place of safety or observation home pending Board inquiry into a criminal allegation against them.
what_it_excludes: A person who has completed eighteen years of age on the date of commission of the offence, even if they appear young or are arrested later.
Children in need of care and protection who are victims or at-risk children not accused of any offence — they fall under the Committee's jurisdiction, not the Board's.
Adults above 21 years who may receive aftercare support under the Act but are no longer within the juvenile definition or jurisdiction of the Juvenile Justice Board.
Persons adjudicated and convicted as adults by the Children's Court after the Board determines them fit for adult trial under section 15 of the Act, though they entered the system as juveniles.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a juvenile determines which forum — the Juvenile Justice Board or a regular criminal court — has jurisdiction over them, and whether punitive adult sentencing or rehabilitative juvenile measures apply. Misclassification can result in unlawful detention of a child in an adult prison or, conversely, incorrect shielding of an adult from due criminal process.

definitions.definition: 'Board' means a Juvenile Justice Board constituted under section 4.
definitions.plain_english: A Juvenile Justice Board is a special court-like body set up in each district of India to handle cases involving children who are accused of committing crimes. It is made up of a judicial magistrate and two social workers, at least one of whom must be a woman. It is designed to be a child-friendly forum that focuses on rehabilitation rather than punishment.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy in Mumbai is arrested for allegedly snatching a mobile phone. Instead of being produced before a regular criminal court, he is brought before the Juvenile Justice Board of Mumbai, which assesses his background through a social investigation report and decides on an appropriate rehabilitation measure.

A 17-year-old girl in Delhi is alleged to have committed a heinous offence. The Juvenile Justice Board first conducts a preliminary assessment under Section 15 to determine whether she has the mental and physical capacity to be tried as an adult, before deciding to transfer the case to the Children's Court.

A child found begging on the streets of Chennai is picked up by police. Upon inquiry, it is discovered the child was coerced by an adult. The Board processes the matter, differentiating the child from an adult offender and directing placement in an observation home while inquiry proceeds.

In a rural district of Rajasthan, a 14-year-old is alleged to have been involved in theft. The Juvenile Justice Board, lacking a regular courtroom, conducts proceedings in a child-friendly setting, ensuring the child is not handcuffed or placed with adult accused, and orders counselling and community service as a corrective measure.

A child in Kolkata is alleged to have committed a petty offence. The Board, after reviewing the social investigation report and consulting with the probation officer, decides to release the child on probation under the supervision of parents rather than sending the child to a special home.
what_it_covers: Cases involving any child alleged to have committed an offence who has not completed eighteen years of age on the date of commission of the offence.
Preliminary assessment proceedings for children alleged to have committed heinous offences to determine if they should be tried as adults.
Orders related to bail, placement in observation homes, and directions for social investigation reports in respect of children in conflict with law.
Conducting inquiries into the circumstances of a child in conflict with law and passing final orders including acquittal, probation, community service, or placement in a special home.
Receiving and acting upon reports from Child Welfare Police Officers and probation officers regarding children brought before it.
what_it_excludes: Cases involving persons who have completed eighteen years of age at the time of commission of the alleged offence, who are tried by regular criminal courts.
Matters relating to children in need of care and protection, which fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Child Welfare Committee and not the Board.
Adoption-related proceedings, which are handled by the Child Welfare Committee and designated courts under the adoption framework of the Act.
Civil or family disputes involving children, such as custody or maintenance matters, which are adjudicated by competent civil courts.
Proceedings against adults who exploit or harm children, which are handled by regular criminal courts or the Children's Court.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a matter is placed before the Juvenile Justice Board determines whether a child receives the procedural protections and rehabilitative focus of the juvenile justice system, including prohibition on imprisonment in an adult jail and eligibility for orders of probation, counselling, or placement in a special home, as opposed to adult criminal prosecution. Non-compliance with the requirement to produce a child before the Board rather than a regular court is a fundamental procedural safeguard whose breach can vitiate the entire proceedings.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, kidnapping in relation to a child or minor means the offences described under sections 359 to 369 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, applied mutatis mutandis to any child or minor under the age of eighteen years, encompassing both kidnapping from India and kidnapping from lawful guardianship, as construed accordingly under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Kidnapping, under the Juvenile Justice Act, means taking away or enticing a child under 18 years of age from the care of their parents or legal guardians without their consent, or taking the child out of India unlawfully. The law borrows its full meaning from the Indian Penal Code's provisions on kidnapping and applies them specifically to protect children. Any person who does this to a child can be prosecuted and punished under these combined provisions.
real_world_examples: A stranger in Delhi lures an 8-year-old girl away from her school with promises of chocolate and takes her to another state without the knowledge or consent of her parents — this constitutes kidnapping from lawful guardianship under the JJ Act read with IPC Section 361.

A relative in Mumbai takes a 15-year-old boy to Dubai without the consent of his father, who is his lawful guardian, for the purpose of forced labour — this amounts to kidnapping from India under IPC Section 360 as applied through Section 84 of the JJ Act.

A trafficker in Chennai persuades a 14-year-old girl to leave her home and accompanies her across state borders under false pretences of a job offer, separating her from her mother — this triggers kidnapping provisions under the JJ Act along with child trafficking offences.

A non-custodial parent in Kolkata forcibly removes a 12-year-old child from the custody of the other parent who holds a court-issued guardianship order, and takes the child to another city — this constitutes kidnapping from lawful guardianship applicable through Section 84 of the JJ Act.

An agent in Hyderabad recruits a 16-year-old tribal girl from her village by deceiving her parents about educational opportunities and transports her to a different state for domestic servitude — kidnapping provisions under Section 84 of the JJ Act apply alongside child labour and trafficking laws.
what_it_covers: Taking or enticing a child under 18 years from the keeping of their lawful guardian without the guardian's consent (kidnapping from lawful guardianship under IPC Section 361 as applied to children).
Conveying a child under 18 years beyond the limits of India without the consent of the person legally authorised to consent on their behalf (kidnapping from India under IPC Section 360).

Using force, compulsion, or deceitful means to take a child under 18 with intent to cause wrongful confinement, grievous hurt, slavery, or illicit intercourse as covered under IPC Sections 363 to 369 applied through Section 84.
Kidnapping a child with intent to commit murder, extort ransom, or subject the child to begging or forced labour as covered under the extended IPC provisions applied mutatis mutandis.
Importing a girl child into India under the age of 18 years for illicit intercourse as criminalised under IPC Section 366B as applied through Section 84 of the JJ Act.
what_it_excludes: Removal of a child by a lawful guardian acting within their legally recognised custodial rights and with proper consent — such acts do not constitute kidnapping under this provision.
Voluntary movement of a child aged 18 years or above, since the Act's application is strictly confined to persons under the age of eighteen years.
Acts of abduction alone that do not involve taking away from lawful guardianship or from India — abduction is separately addressed and not automatically synonymous with kidnapping under this Act.
Custodial removal of a child by a State authority acting under a valid court order or under the provisions of the JJ Act itself, such as placement in a Child Care Institution.
Civil custody or guardianship disputes resolved under family law or the Guardians and Wards Act that do not involve criminal intent or force.
definitions.why_it_matters: The application of this definition triggers serious criminal liability — including cognizable and non-bailable offences — under the IPC as read with the JJ Act, enabling police to arrest without a warrant and courts to impose imprisonment up to seven years or more depending on the specific IPC section invoked. It also determines whether a child victim becomes entitled to protective interventions, rehabilitation, and restoration under the JJ Act's child protection framework.

definitions.definition: A 'lawful guardian' means any person who is lawfully entrusted with the care and custody of a child by operation of law, court order, or legal instrument, and whose authority to act as guardian is recognised under applicable Indian law. For the purposes of Section 84, the term is used in the context of sections 359 to 369 of the Indian Penal Code, as applied mutatis mutandis to persons under eighteen years of age, to distinguish authorised custodians from those who unlawfully take or entice a child away.
definitions.plain_english: A lawful guardian is any person who has been legally given the responsibility to look after a child. This could be someone appointed by a court, a government authority, or recognised under personal law. The key point is that their authority over the child is official and legally valid — not merely a social or informal arrangement.
real_world_examples: A court in Delhi appoints a maternal uncle as the legal guardian of a 10-year-old orphan under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890; that uncle is the lawful guardian for purposes of Section 84.

A Child Welfare Committee in Mumbai places a child in need of care and protection in a Children's Home; the Superintendent of that Home acts as the lawful guardian of the child during the period of institutional care.

A District Magistrate in Chennai passes an order under the Juvenile Justice Act granting foster care of a surrendered child to a foster family; the foster parents become the lawful guardians of that child.

A Sessions Court in Kolkata, during a custody dispute, issues an interim order granting the mother exclusive custody of a 14-year-old; the mother is the lawful guardian and any person taking the child away without her consent may be liable under the kidnapping provisions applied via Section 84.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Hyderabad holds a child declared legally free for adoption; until the adoption order is passed, the Agency's head acts as lawful guardian under the applicable Juvenile Justice framework.

A probation officer in Bengaluru is formally entrusted with the supervision and care of a child in conflict with law released on bail; for the duration of that order, the probation officer's institutional authority qualifies as that of a lawful guardian.
what_it_covers: A guardian appointed by a competent court under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 for a child below 18 years.
A Child Care Institution, Children's Home, or Specialised Adoption Agency officially entrusted with custody of a child under an order of the Child Welfare Committee or Juvenile Justice Board.
A foster family or fit person formally designated by a competent authority under the Juvenile Justice Act with lawful custody of a child.
A natural parent whose parental rights and custody are recognised and undisturbed by any court order, thereby making them the default lawful guardian.
A probation officer or government-appointed custodian acting under a specific court or statutory order for a child in conflict with law.
what_it_excludes: A person who merely has a social, customary, or informal arrangement to look after a child without any legal recognition or court order.
A biological relative such as a grandparent, aunt, or neighbour who looks after a child voluntarily but without formal guardianship order or legal instrument.
A person who was previously a lawful guardian but whose guardianship has been revoked or superseded by a subsequent court order.
An employer or school authority who has temporary day-to-day charge of a child but no legal guardianship status.
A person claiming guardianship based solely on religious or customary practice that has not been validated by a court or competent authority under applicable law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the lawful guardian is decisive in determining whether the offences of kidnapping or abduction under IPC sections 359 to 369, as applied via Section 84, are committed — taking a child without the consent of the lawful guardian constitutes kidnapping from lawful guardianship, attracting serious criminal liability. Conversely, a person who is not recognised as a lawful guardian cannot trigger these protections, and unauthorised removal of the child by the actual lawful guardian from an unlawful custodian may be a lawful act.

definitions.definition: 'Child legally free for adoption' means a child declared as such by the Committee after making due inquiry under section 38.
definitions.plain_english: A child is 'legally free for adoption' when the Child Welfare Committee has officially declared, after a proper investigation, that the child can be adopted. This declaration is made for children who are orphaned, abandoned, or surrendered by their biological parents. Only after this declaration can the formal adoption process begin for that child.
real_world_examples: A newborn infant found abandoned at a railway station in Mumbai is brought before the Child Welfare Committee. After due inquiry confirming no traceable biological parents, the Committee declares the child legally free for adoption, enabling a Specialised Adoption Agency to place the child on the adoption platform CARINGS.

A couple in Gujarat surrenders their two-year-old daughter by executing a surrender deed before the Child Welfare Committee, citing extreme poverty and inability to care for her. After the mandatory two-month reconsideration period lapses without the parents reclaiming the child, the Committee declares the child legally free for adoption.

A five-year-old orphan in a Children's Home in Chennai, both of whose parents died in a road accident and who has no surviving relatives willing to take guardianship, is presented before the Child Welfare Committee. After inquiries with extended family and local authorities yield no willing caretakers, the Committee passes a formal order declaring the child legally free for adoption.

An abandoned child found near a temple in Kolkata is initially placed in a Specialised Adoption Agency. After a two-month waiting period during which newspaper notices and police reports fail to trace any biological parent or guardian, the Child Welfare Committee conducts its inquiry and issues a declaration that the child is legally free for adoption.

A seven-year-old child in Rajasthan, whose single mother was declared by the Committee as unfit due to severe mental illness with no other family support, is formally declared legally free for adoption by the Child Welfare Committee following a thorough social investigation, enabling in-country adoption proceedings to commence.
what_it_covers: An orphaned child with no surviving biological parents or willing relatives, declared legally free for adoption by the Committee after due inquiry.
An abandoned child who has been declared abandoned by the Committee after a mandatory waiting and inquiry period, with no biological parents or guardians coming forward to claim the child.

A surrendered child whose biological parents have executed a valid surrender deed before the Committee and have not reclaimed the child within the prescribed reconsideration period, following which the Committee issues the declaration.
A child placed in a Specialised Adoption Agency whose biological family cannot be traced despite all prescribed efforts, and the Committee formally declares the child free for adoption.

A child whose parents have been found unfit or incapacitated by the Committee and where no alternative family care arrangement is possible, rendering the child eligible for a legally free for adoption declaration.
what_it_excludes: A child who is merely in institutional care or a Children's Home but has not yet received a formal declaration from the Child Welfare Committee is not legally free for adoption.
A child with traceable biological parents or guardians who are willing and capable of caring for the child, even if the child is temporarily in State care.
A child in respect of whom the Child Welfare Committee has not yet conducted or concluded the due inquiry under section 38, regardless of the child's orphan, abandoned, or surrendered status.

A child who is a 'child in conflict with law' under the jurisdiction of the Juvenile Justice Board, as such children are not categorised under child welfare proceedings that lead to adoption declarations.

A child whose biological parents have surrendered the child but are still within the statutory reconsideration period permitted by law to reclaim the child, as the declaration cannot be made until that period expires.
definitions.why_it_matters: This declaration is the mandatory legal prerequisite that unlocks the formal adoption process under sections 58, 59, and 66 of the Act — without it, no prospective adoptive parent (whether Indian resident, non-resident Indian, or foreign) can legally adopt the child, and any purported adoption would be void. It directly determines which children can be matched with and placed for adoption through the Central Adoption Resource Authority, and governs inter-country adoption eligibility under section 59.

definitions.definition: Every institution registered under the Juvenile Justice Act shall have a Management Committee, to be set up in a manner as may be prescribed, to manage the institution and monitor the progress of every child housed therein.
definitions.plain_english: A Management Committee is a mandatory governing body that must be established in every registered child care institution under the Juvenile Justice Act. Its two core duties are to run the day-to-day operations of the institution and to keep track of how each individual child in the institution is progressing. The exact way it is formed and how it works is decided by rules made by the State Government.
real_world_examples: A Government-run Children's Home in Lucknow constitutes a Management Committee comprising the officer-in-charge, a social worker, a medical officer and a representative of the District Child Protection Unit to oversee daily administration and review individual care plans of every child resident.

A registered NGO-run special home for girls in conflict with law in Mumbai sets up a Management Committee that meets monthly to assess each girl's rehabilitation progress, approve skill-development programmes and ensure compliance with prescribed standards of food, shelter and medical care.

A Specialised Adoption Agency in Chennai operating a residential facility for abandoned children below six years forms a Management Committee that monitors nutrition records, facilitates birth registration for unregistered children and coordinates referral services for medical treatment.

An observation home in Kolkata establishes a Management Committee that reviews individual care plans prepared for newly admitted children in conflict with law, oversees occupational therapy schedules and tracks educational enrolment under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.

A place of safety in Bhopal housing children who have committed heinous offences constitutes a Management Committee that coordinates with legal aid providers, supervises mental health counselling sessions and submits periodic progress reports to the Juvenile Justice Board and the District Magistrate.
what_it_covers: Every institution registered under the Juvenile Justice Act, including Children's Homes, special homes, observation homes, places of safety and Specialised Adoption Agencies that house children.

The function of managing the institution — including overseeing basic requirements such as food, shelter, clothing, medical attention, education, skill development, mental health interventions and recreational activities.
The function of monitoring the progress of every individual child in the institution, including review of individual care plans, follow-up on rehabilitation goals and tracking reintegration outcomes.
Setting up of the committee in accordance with the manner prescribed by State Government rules, which may specify composition, frequency of meetings and reporting obligations.
Coordination with external service providers for referral services such as vocational training, de-addiction, legal aid and treatment of diseases as part of comprehensive case management.
what_it_excludes: Children's committees formed under Section 53(3) for children above six years of age, which are separate participatory bodies distinct from the Management Committee.

The Child Welfare Committee, which is a statutory quasi-judicial authority constituted under Section 27 for making decisions about children in need of care and protection, not for managing an institution.
The Inspection Committee or State-level monitoring bodies constituted under other provisions of the Act, which inspect institutions from outside rather than managing them internally.
Informal or ad hoc advisory groups or parent-teacher style bodies that may exist in a facility but are not formally constituted under the prescribed rules as a Management Committee.

Boards of trustees or governing councils of the parent NGO or registered society that owns and operates the institution, which operate under separate legal frameworks such as the Societies Registration Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and functioning of a Management Committee is a mandatory statutory requirement for every registered institution; failure to constitute one or non-compliance with its duties can expose an institution to cancellation of registration, penalties or adverse orders by the Board or Child Welfare Committee. The Management Committee directly determines whether children receive prescribed rehabilitation services, individual care plans are followed, and progress is monitored — making it the primary accountability mechanism for the institutional care of every child.

definitions.definition: A 'medical practitioner' means a person who holds a recognised medical qualification and is duly registered under the applicable law to practise medicine in India, including the authority to examine patients, certify medical conditions, and prescribe treatment. In the context of the Juvenile Justice Act, the term is used specifically to denote a qualified and registered medical professional whose certification or order carries legal weight, such as certifying disability in a child (Section 85) or authorising the administration of intoxicating liquor, narcotic drugs, or psychotropic substances to a child for medical purposes (Section 77).
definitions.plain_english: A medical practitioner is a properly trained and officially registered doctor or physician who is legally allowed to examine patients and provide medical treatment in India. In the Juvenile Justice Act, a medical practitioner plays an important role in two key situations: authorising the use of controlled substances for a sick child, and officially certifying that a child has a disability. Only someone with this recognised medical qualification and registration can make these legally binding decisions under the Act.
real_world_examples: A government-run children's home in Mumbai administers a prescribed sedative to a child with severe epilepsy — the administration is lawful only because a registered MBBS doctor at a nearby public hospital has written a formal medical order for it under Section 77.

A Child Welfare Committee in Chennai is examining a case where an abuser physically assaulted a child who has cerebral palsy. A registered medical officer from a government hospital issues a disability certificate confirming the child's condition, thereby triggering the doubled penalty under Section 85.

A registered paediatrician at AIIMS Delhi certifies in writing that a child in a special care unit requires a small quantity of alcohol-based tonic as part of a prescribed treatment, providing legal cover to the nursing staff administering it under Section 77.

In a case before the Juvenile Justice Board in Kolkata, the prosecution relies on a disability certificate issued by an orthopaedic surgeon registered under the West Bengal Medical Council to establish that the child victim had a locomotor disability, qualifying the offender for enhanced punishment under Section 85.

A registered Ayurvedic practitioner (holding a recognised BAMS degree and registered under a State Medical Council) certifies a child's disability in a rural district in Rajasthan, raising a legal question before the District Magistrate about whether such certification qualifies under the Act's reference to a 'medical practitioner'.

During a rescue operation in Hyderabad, a forensic medical officer from a government hospital examines a trafficked child with a visual impairment and issues a formal disability certificate, which the Child Welfare Committee uses to invoke the enhanced penalty provisions of Section 85 against the traffickers.
what_it_covers: A registered allopathic doctor (MBBS or higher) registered under the Medical Council of India or a State Medical Council who certifies a child's disability under Section 85.
A duly qualified physician whose written order lawfully permits administration of intoxicating liquor, narcotic drugs, or psychotropic substances to a child under Section 77.

Specialists such as orthopaedic surgeons, neurologists, or psychiatrists who hold recognised medical qualifications and are registered to practise, and who issue formal disability certificates for child victims.

Practitioners registered under recognised Indian medical systems (such as BAMS or BHMS) where their qualifications are recognised under applicable law and they are duly registered with the relevant state or national council.
what_it_excludes: Unregistered or unqualified individuals who may possess some medical knowledge but hold no recognised degree or current registration with a Medical Council.
Pharmacists, nurses, paramedics, or health workers who are not independently licensed to diagnose, certify disability, or prescribe controlled substances under applicable law.
Traditional healers, faith healers, or homeopathic practitioners whose qualifications are not formally recognised under any statute governing medical practice in India.
A lapsed or de-registered medical practitioner whose registration has been cancelled or suspended by the Medical Council at the time of issuing the certificate or order.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'medical practitioner' is legally decisive in two situations: first, under Section 77, only an order from such a person exempts the giver of intoxicating liquor, narcotic drugs, or psychotropic substances to a child from criminal liability carrying up to seven years' rigorous imprisonment; second, under Section 85, only a certificate from such a person can establish a child's disability, which doubles the penalty for any offence committed against that child under the chapter.

definitions.definition: 'Mentally ill person' shall have the same meaning assigned to it in clause (l) of section 2 of the Mental Health Act, 1987 (14 of 1987), as applied within the context of Section 93 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'mentally ill person' in this law refers to a child who has a mental disorder or condition that affects their mental functioning, as defined under India's Mental Health Act, 1987. This means the child is suffering from a recognised psychiatric illness or disorder. When a child in a juvenile care institution is found to be mentally ill, the authorities can transfer them to a proper psychiatric facility for treatment.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy held in an observation home in Mumbai is found exhibiting symptoms of schizophrenia — hearing voices, paranoid behaviour, and inability to communicate coherently — leading the Juvenile Justice Board to order his transfer to a government psychiatric hospital under Section 93.

A girl in a Children's Home in Delhi shows signs of severe bipolar disorder with violent mood swings and self-harm tendencies; the Child Welfare Committee certifies her as a mentally ill person and arranges her admission to a psychiatric nursing home for inpatient treatment.

A 12-year-old child rescued from a trafficking ring in Kolkata and placed in a special home is diagnosed with severe post-traumatic stress disorder and psychosis; the Board classifies her as a mentally ill person and transfers her to a psychiatric facility for specialised care.

A child in conflict with law lodged in a special home in Chennai displays symptoms of severe depression with psychotic features; upon evaluation by a psychiatrist, the Juvenile Justice Board invokes Section 93 to transfer the child to the Institute of Mental Health for treatment.

A 14-year-old boy in an observation home in Pune is found to suffer from acute anxiety disorder combined with substance-induced psychosis following years of solvent abuse; the Board, treating him as a mentally ill person, orders his removal to a psychiatric nursing home before further referral to an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts.
what_it_covers: A child in a juvenile care institution diagnosed with a recognised mental disorder such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or severe depression as defined under the Mental Health Act, 1987.
A child exhibiting psychosis or other psychiatric conditions that impair their mental functioning and require inpatient psychiatric treatment.
A child whose mental illness is certified by a medical professional and who consequently qualifies for transfer to a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric nursing home under Section 93.

Children suffering from substance-induced psychiatric disorders where the mental illness is the primary concern warranting psychiatric hospitalisation, as referenced in the dual-use of this definition within Section 93.
what_it_excludes: Children who are merely addicted to alcohol or other drugs but do not exhibit a concurrent diagnosable mental illness as defined under the Mental Health Act, 1987 — such children are covered separately under the addiction limb of Section 93.
Children with intellectual disabilities or developmental disorders (such as autism spectrum disorder) that are not classified as mental illness under the Mental Health Act, 1987.

Children displaying temporary behavioural problems, emotional disturbances, or conduct disorders that do not meet the clinical threshold of 'mental illness' under clause (l) of section 2 of the Mental Health Act, 1987.
Children who have recovered from a mental illness and have been discharged from psychiatric care — once discharged, they revert to standard juvenile justice procedures unless the condition recurs.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a child qualifies as a 'mentally ill person' under this definition directly determines whether the Committee or Board has the legal authority to order the child's removal from a juvenile care institution to a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric nursing home under Section 93. This classification triggers a mandatory transfer mechanism and dictates the duration of treatment, limiting institutionalisation to only the period required for inpatient psychiatric care.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 84 of the Juvenile Justice Act, a 'minor' means a person who is under the age of eighteen years, to whom the provisions of sections 359 to 369 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) relating to kidnapping and abduction apply mutatis mutandis.
definitions.plain_english: A 'minor' under this law refers to any person who has not yet completed eighteen years of age. This term is specifically used in the context of kidnapping and abduction offences, ensuring that the protections under the Indian Penal Code for kidnapping and abduction extend to all individuals below eighteen years. In simple terms, any child or young person under 18 is treated as a 'minor' for the purpose of these offences.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old girl from Bihar is lured away from her home by a trafficker promising employment in a city — she qualifies as a 'minor' and the kidnapping provisions of the IPC apply fully to protect her under Section 84.

A 10-year-old boy in Mumbai is taken away from his school by an unknown person without the consent of his parents — this constitutes abduction of a minor and the Juvenile Justice Act read with IPC sections 359-369 applies.

A 17-year-old in Delhi is persuaded by an adult to leave her guardian's custody and cross state lines — being under 18, she is a 'minor' and the person who induced her can be prosecuted for kidnapping under the mutatis mutandis application of the IPC.

A 12-year-old orphan in Chennai is taken away from a registered children's home by an unauthorised person — the child being a minor attracts the kidnapping and abduction provisions applicable under Section 84 of the Juvenile Justice Act.

A couple in Rajasthan abducts a 16-year-old for the purpose of forced marriage — the victim being under 18 years is classified as a minor, triggering IPC sections on kidnapping for marriage as applicable under the Juvenile Justice Act.
what_it_covers: Any individual under the age of 18 years who is the victim of kidnapping or abduction as defined under IPC sections 359 to 369.
A child below 18 who is taken or enticed away from lawful guardianship without consent, whether male or female.
A 'minor' who is kidnapped across state or international borders, attracting the full range of IPC provisions as adapted under Section 84.
A minor who has been abducted for purposes such as forced labour, trafficking, marriage, or ransom, irrespective of whether they are an orphan, abandoned child, or in institutional care.
what_it_excludes: Any person who has attained the age of eighteen years or above, as they fall outside the definition of 'minor' under Section 84.
Adults who are voluntarily accompanying another adult without any coercion or inducement, even if the circumstances seem irregular.
Cases where a parent or legal guardian moves a child in accordance with lawful custody rights, as such movement does not constitute kidnapping or abduction of a minor.
Offences unrelated to kidnapping and abduction — the term 'minor' in this section has no bearing on other parts of the Juvenile Justice Act outside Section 84.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'minor' under Section 84 determines whether the kidnapping and abduction provisions of IPC sections 359 to 369 can be applied to protect them — a finding that the victim is under 18 makes the accused liable for the full range of kidnapping and abduction offences as adapted under the Juvenile Justice Act, including offences attracting imprisonment of up to seven years or more. This classification also ensures that law enforcement and courts treat such cases with the heightened seriousness mandated for crimes against children.
