definitions.term: State Commission for Protection of Child Rights
definitions.definition: The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights constituted under section 17 of the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 (4 of 2006), which, in addition to its functions under that Act, is mandated to monitor the implementation of the provisions of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act in such manner as may be prescribed, and shall have the same powers vested in it under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 while inquiring into any matter relating to any offence under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights is a body set up in each state to protect the rights of children. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, it is given the additional responsibility of keeping a watch on how the state is following and implementing the law meant to care for children in need and children in conflict with the law. It has the power to investigate offences and must include its work under this law in its annual report.
real_world_examples: The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights in Maharashtra conducts an inspection of observation homes across Mumbai to verify whether children in conflict with law are being housed and cared for as required under the Juvenile Justice Act, and submits its findings in its annual report.

In Rajasthan, a complaint is received that a Child Care Institution is exploiting children by engaging them in child labour; the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights exercises its powers to inquire into the matter and takes action as permitted under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005.

The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights in Tamil Nadu monitors whether District Child Protection Units across the state are functioning effectively, reviewing records of children in need of care and protection who were produced before Child Welfare Committees.

Following media reports of abuse in a special home for children in Uttar Pradesh, the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights suo motu takes up the matter, summons officials, and recommends remedial action to the State Government, recording its activities in its mandatory annual report.

The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights in West Bengal tracks the implementation of after care programs for children aging out of institutional care and reports gaps in the system to the state legislature through its annual report as required under section 16 of the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005.
what_it_covers: Monitoring the implementation of all provisions of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act within the state, including functioning of Child Care Institutions, Juvenile Justice Boards, and Child Welfare Committees.

Inquiring into matters relating to any offence under the Juvenile Justice Act, exercising the same powers available to it under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, such as summoning witnesses, inspecting premises, and calling for documents.

Including its activities carried out under section 109 of the Juvenile Justice Act in the annual report submitted under section 16 of the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, ensuring legislative transparency and accountability.

Reviewing complaints or reports of violations of children's rights arising from failure to comply with the Juvenile Justice Act, including neglect in observation homes, special homes, or child care institutions.
what_it_excludes: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, which is a separate body constituted under section 3 of the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, and operates at the national level independently of the State Commission.

Judicial functions and adjudication of offences, which remain exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Children's Court, Juvenile Justice Board, and other competent courts established under the Juvenile Justice Act.

Administrative child protection functions such as registering adoption agencies, issuing no objection certificates, or passing adoption orders, which are assigned to specific authorities like the Central Adoption Resource Authority or competent authorities under the Act.

Functions of the District Child Protection Unit or District Magistrate in direct case management and placement of children, which are field-level executive responsibilities distinct from the State Commission's oversight and monitoring role.
definitions.why_it_matters: The State Commission for Protection of Child Rights serves as the principal state-level oversight mechanism ensuring that child-centric provisions of the Juvenile Justice Act are actually implemented on the ground; its powers to inquire into offences and compel accountability mean that institutional failures, abuse in child care institutions, or systemic non-compliance can be formally investigated and remedied. Its annual reporting obligation creates a public accountability record that can influence state policy, legislative amendments, and judicial interventions concerning child rights.

definitions.definition: 'State Government' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, but as used throughout the Act, it refers to the government of each State of India or Union Territory (with legislature) that exercises legislative and executive authority within its territorial jurisdiction for the purposes of implementation, administration, and enforcement of the provisions of this Act, including the establishment and maintenance of institutional infrastructure for children.
definitions.plain_english: The 'State Government' refers to the elected government of any Indian state or union territory that is responsible for running government affairs within that state. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, it is the State Government that must set up homes for children, appoint officials, register institutions, and fund programs that protect and rehabilitate children in need. Essentially, it is the local governing authority at the state level that ensures the law is put into practice on the ground.
real_world_examples: The Government of Maharashtra sets up and funds Observation Homes and Special Homes across districts in Maharashtra under Section 44 to house children in conflict with law during inquiry proceedings.

The Government of Tamil Nadu, acting as the State Government, registers non-governmental organisations to run Children's Homes and Specialised Adoption Agencies within Tamil Nadu's territorial jurisdiction.

The Delhi government (NCT of Delhi), as the State Government for a Union Territory with legislature, establishes District Child Protection Units and appoints Child Welfare Police Officers across Delhi districts.

The Government of Uttar Pradesh, pursuant to its obligations under Section 44, provides financial grants and infrastructure support for the maintenance of Place of Safety facilities for children above 16 years involved in heinous offences.

The Government of Rajasthan frames state-specific rules under the Juvenile Justice Act, prescribes standards for child care institutions, and notifies the inspection committees responsible for oversight in Rajasthan.
what_it_covers: The elected government and its executive apparatus of any of the 28 states of India responsible for implementing the Juvenile Justice Act within their respective territories.
Union Territories with their own legislatures, such as Delhi and Puducherry, which exercise state-like governmental authority for the purposes of this Act.

The administrative machinery of a state government — including departments of Women and Child Development — that establishes, registers, maintains, funds, and oversees child care institutions under Section 44 and related provisions.
State governments exercising their delegated rule-making power to frame state-level rules and procedures supplementing the central framework of the Act.
what_it_excludes: The Central Government of India, which is a separate and distinct authority with its own obligations under the Act, including framing adoption regulations and constituting the Central Adoption Resource Authority.

Union Territories without legislatures (such as Lakshadweep or Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu), where the Central Government effectively exercises state-level powers and the term 'State Government' must be read accordingly.
Local self-government bodies such as Municipal Corporations, Panchayats, or District Boards, which are subordinate entities and do not constitute the 'State Government' for purposes of this Act.
Autonomous bodies, registered societies, or non-governmental organisations even if fully funded by the state, as they are distinct legal entities from the State Government itself.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of 'State Government' is critical because Section 44 and numerous other provisions impose direct mandatory obligations — such as establishing Observation Homes, Special Homes, and Places of Safety — exclusively on the State Government, making it legally accountable for non-compliance and empowering courts to compel performance; failure to distinguish the State Government from other bodies could nullify enforcement of these obligations and the child welfare rights they underpin.

definitions.definition: A surrender deed is a formal legal document executed by a parent or guardian before the Child Welfare Committee, surrendering a child whom they are unable to care for due to physical, emotional, or social factors beyond their control, and upon execution of which the Committee certifies the voluntary relinquishment and provides a two-month reconsideration period before any further proceedings.
definitions.plain_english: A surrender deed is an official written document signed by a parent or guardian in front of the Child Welfare Committee when they are unable to look after their child due to serious personal hardships. It is not an immediate permanent act — the parents are given two months to change their mind after signing. The Committee must certify that the decision was made voluntarily and ensure all efforts have been made to keep the family together before the child can eventually be declared free for adoption.
real_world_examples: A single mother in Chennai suffering from a terminal illness and with no family support produces her two-year-old child before the Child Welfare Committee and, after counselling, signs a surrender deed because she cannot physically or financially care for the child.

A daily-wage labourer couple in Rajasthan, facing extreme poverty and unable to feed their newborn, appears before the Committee; after inquiry and counselling they execute a surrender deed, following which the infant is placed in a Specialised Adoption Agency during the two-month reconsideration period.

A survivor of trafficking in Mumbai, psychologically traumatised and homeless, surrenders her infant before the local Child Welfare Committee; the Committee certifies the surrender deed and ensures she is given counselling and two months to reconsider while the child is placed in supervised care.

A guardian in Kolkata who is the sole caretaker of a child but has developed a severe disability rendering them incapable of care, formally executes a surrender deed before the Committee after social investigation confirms the hardship, initiating the process toward declaring the child legally free for adoption.

A couple in rural Uttar Pradesh with four children and no stable income surrenders their youngest child; the Committee first directs social investigation, then after counselling certifies the surrender deed, noting all family restoration options were exhausted before proceeding.
what_it_covers: Formal voluntary relinquishment of a child by a biological parent before the Child Welfare Committee after mandatory counselling and inquiry.
Relinquishment by a legal guardian who is unable to care for the child due to physical, emotional, or social factors beyond their control.

The certified document that initiates the two-month reconsideration period and subsequent placement of the child in a Specialised Adoption Agency (if below six years) or children's home (if above six years).
Cases where both parents or a single surviving parent are incapable of care and the Committee has verified through social investigation that restoration or family support is not feasible.
The trigger document that enables the Committee to later declare a child as a surrendered child and, after due inquiry, as legally free for adoption.
what_it_excludes: Informal or oral relinquishment of a child without appearing before the Child Welfare Committee — such acts do not constitute a valid surrender deed.
Abandonment of a child without the parent or guardian's appearance before the Committee — abandoned children are governed by a separate classification and process.
Surrender executed under coercion, fraud, or undue influence — the Committee must certify voluntariness, and any such deed would be invalid.
Transfer of custody through private arrangements, court orders in matrimonial disputes, or adoption orders — these are distinct legal processes not governed by the surrender deed mechanism.
Surrenders attempted without completion of the mandatory inquiry and counselling process — the deed is not valid unless the Committee is satisfied and certifies execution.
definitions.why_it_matters: Execution of a surrender deed is the legally required prerequisite that classifies a child as a 'surrendered child' under the Act, enabling the Committee to eventually declare the child legally free for adoption after the two-month reconsideration period; without a certified surrender deed, the child cannot be processed through the adoption pipeline and the Committee cannot direct institutional or foster placement on surrendered-child grounds.

definitions.definition: The term 'victim' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; however, as used in Section 99, a 'victim' means a child who has suffered harm, injury, abuse, exploitation, or deprivation of rights as a consequence of an act or omission constituting an offence or violation under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.
definitions.plain_english: A 'victim' in the context of the Juvenile Justice Act refers to a child who has been harmed, abused, exploited, or wronged because of someone else's actions or failures. This includes children who have suffered physical, emotional, sexual, or financial harm. The Act ensures such children can receive support, compensation, and rehabilitation through the legal system.
real_world_examples: A 10-year-old girl in Mumbai who was sexually abused by a neighbour is a victim under the Act; she can be referred by the Child Welfare Committee to receive compensation and counselling services under Section 99.
A 14-year-old boy in Bihar trafficked to work in a brick kiln factory is a victim of exploitation, entitling him to rehabilitation, restoration to family, and potential compensation under the Act.

A 7-year-old child in Delhi found begging under coercion by a gang, suffering physical abuse when targets were not met, qualifies as a victim whose case is taken up by the Child Welfare Committee for protection and relief.

A 16-year-old girl in Rajasthan whose family arranged her child marriage, exposing her to harm, is treated as a victim under the Act, triggering intervention by authorities and eligibility for support services.

A 12-year-old orphan in Chennai who was lured and subjected to online sexual exploitation is recognised as a victim, enabling referral to a Children's Home, legal aid, and compensation under the applicable provisions.
what_it_covers: A child who has suffered physical, sexual, emotional, or psychological harm due to an act or omission by any person under this Act or any other applicable law.
A child who has been trafficked, exploited for labour or sexual purposes, or subjected to abuse within or outside a household.
A child who has been harmed as a result of neglect, abandonment, or wilful failure of a guardian or parent to provide care and protection.
A child affected by armed conflict, civil unrest, or natural calamity who has suffered deprivation of rights and basic needs.
A child who has been subjected to illegal acts such as drug induction or forced begging, resulting in demonstrable harm.
what_it_excludes: A child in conflict with law who is the alleged offender in a case, even if they subsequently suffer hardship during the justice process.
An adult (person who has completed eighteen years of age) who suffered harm as a minor but is no longer within the age jurisdiction of the Act at the time of proceedings.
A person who has suffered purely economic or property harm without any corresponding personal injury, abuse, or deprivation of rights as a child.
A witness to a crime involving a child who is not themselves the direct recipient of harm, abuse, or exploitation.

A prospective adoptive parent or foster carer who claims to have been wronged in an administrative process under the Act, as they do not fall within the child-centric scope of victimhood under this provision.

definitions.definition: A voluntary organisation, as used in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, refers to any non-governmental or voluntary body registered under any law for the time being in force in India, which may be recognised by the Board or the Committee as a fit facility to temporarily take the responsibility of a child for a specific purpose, subject to due inquiry regarding the suitability of the facility and the organisation to care for the child.
definitions.plain_english: A voluntary organisation is a non-profit or non-governmental group that is officially registered under Indian law and works to help children in need. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, such organisations can be approved by the Juvenile Justice Board or Child Welfare Committee to temporarily look after a child for a specific reason. The government checks whether the organisation and its facility are suitable before granting this recognition, and can cancel it if needed.
real_world_examples: An NGO called 'Bal Ashray' registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 in Pune, which runs a shelter for street children, is recognised by the Child Welfare Committee as a fit facility to temporarily house a child found begging on the streets.

A charitable trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act operating a rehabilitation centre in Delhi for children rescued from trafficking is approved by the Juvenile Justice Board to temporarily care for a child victim while the inquiry is pending.

A voluntary organisation registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 in Chennai that runs a child care home is recognised by the Committee to provide temporary shelter to an abandoned child until a more permanent placement is arranged.

A non-governmental organisation registered under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) running a skill development and after-care programme in Kolkata is approved by the Board to temporarily take custody of a child in conflict with law for specific rehabilitative purposes.

A faith-based charitable society registered under the Karnataka Societies Registration Act operating an open shelter in Bengaluru is recognised by the Child Welfare Committee as a fit facility to temporarily accommodate children in need of care and protection rescued during a police raid.
what_it_covers: Any non-governmental organisation or charitable trust registered under a statute such as the Societies Registration Act, 1860, Companies Act, 2013, or Indian Trusts Act that runs a child care facility.

A voluntary body registered under any state or central legislation in force in India that has been found suitable through due inquiry to temporarily care for a child for a specific purpose directed by the Board or Committee.
Non-profit organisations running open shelters, rehabilitation centres, observation homes, or similar facilities that apply for and receive recognition under Section 51 of the Act.
Organisations registered under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) or similar laws operating child welfare programmes and seeking fit facility recognition from the Board or Committee.
what_it_excludes: Unregistered informal groups or community bodies that have not obtained registration under any law, as the Act expressly requires the organisation to be registered under any law for the time being in force.
For-profit private companies or commercial entities running child care facilities, as the term is confined to voluntary or non-governmental organisations without a profit motive.
Governmental organisations, which are separately categorised under Section 51 and are distinct from voluntary or non-governmental organisations in the Act's framework.
Individuals acting in a personal capacity as fit persons, who are governed separately under the Act and do not qualify as a voluntary organisation.
Organisations that have had their recognition withdrawn by the Board or Committee under Section 51(2) due to recorded reasons of unsuitability.
definitions.why_it_matters: Recognition of a voluntary organisation as a fit facility under Section 51 is the legal gateway that authorises it to temporarily take responsibility for a child under the juvenile justice system; without such recognition, an organisation has no lawful authority to receive or care for a child directed to it by the Board or Committee. Conversely, withdrawal of recognition immediately strips the organisation of this authority, making any subsequent custody of a child without fresh recognition potentially unlawful.

definitions.definition: Wilful neglect, as used in Section 75 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, means a deliberate and intentional failure by a person having actual charge of or control over a child to provide the care, supervision, or necessities required for the child's well-being, in a manner likely to cause unnecessary mental or physical suffering to the child.
